title: What to know about the landmark Warner Bros. Discovery sale
snippet: Learn more about Paramount's planned acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery — a historic Hollywood megadeal valued at $111 billion — as it continues to develop.
fullText:
Earlier this year, the streaming and entertainment industry witnessed one of its most high-stakes megadeals ever, stunning industry observers. Not only is it historic in its size, but it is also predicted to disrupt Hollywood and the media business as we know it. 

After years of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) struggling under the weight of billions of dollars in debt, compounded by declining cable viewership and fierce competition from streaming platforms, the company has been considering major strategic changes, including selling its entertainment assets to one of its rivals.

Several major players saw the potential in acquiring the media giant, and in December, Netflix announced it would acquire WBD’s studios and streaming for $82.7 billion.

But in a surprise eleventh-hour move in late February, the David Ellison-run Paramount became the winner of this bidding war, offering $111 billion to acquire all of WBD’s assets, including its studios, HBO, streaming platforms, games, and TV networks such as CNN and HGTV. Paramount was recently acquired by Ellison with significant support from his father, Larry Ellison — the Oracle chairman, world’s sixth-richest person, and major Trump donor.

Paramount’s offer was approved by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) in June. A federal judge then paused the deal after a lawsuit was filed on July 13 by a coalition of 12 state attorneys general. However, a judge approved it in late September, with the acquisition finally official as of October 6. 

Let’s break down exactly what happened and what could come next. 

What has happened so far?

​This all started back in October 2025 when Warner Bros. Discovery revealed it was exploring a potential sale after receiving unsolicited interest from several major players in the industry.

​The bidding process quickly became competitive, and Paramount and Comcast emerged as serious contenders, with Paramount initially viewed as the frontrunner. 

However, WBD’s board eventually determined that an offer from the streaming giant Netflix was the most attractive. Netflix offered $82.7 billion for just Warner’s film, television, and streaming assets.

Thus began the bidding war. Paramount believed its bid of approximately $108 billion for all of Warner’s assets was superior to Netflix’s offer that focused on just the studios and streaming. To sweeten its deal, Netflix amended its agreement in January to an all-cash offer at $27.75 per share of Warner Bros. Discovery, further reassuring investors and paving the way for the deal to proceed.

​Paramount persisted in its attempts to acquire WBD. Still, the Warner board repeatedly rejected its offers, citing concerns about Paramount’s heavy debt load and the increased risk associated with its proposal, including concern over the suite of investors bankrolling Paramount’s bid, which includes Saudi, Qatari, and Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth funds. The board noted that Paramount’s offer would have left the combined company burdened with $87 billion in debt, a risk they were unwilling to take at the time.

In January, Paramount filed a lawsuit seeking more information about the Netflix deal. A month later, the company sought to sweeten its deal by announcing it would offer a $0.25 per share “ticking fee” to WBD shareholders for each quarter the deal fails to close by December 31, 2026. It also said it would pay the $2.8 billion breakup fee if Warner backs out of its deal with Netflix.

Then, in a final attempt to secure a deal, Paramount increased its offer to $31 per share in February. This prompted the WBD board to prolong discussions with Paramount regarding a potential agreement, considering it as a superior offer. Netflix declined to increase its bid and withdrew from the negotiations.

“The transaction we negotiated would have created shareholder value with a clear path to regulatory approval,” Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said in a statement on February 26. “However, we’ve always been disciplined, and at the price required to match Paramount Skydance’s latest offer, the deal is no longer financially attractive, so we are declining to match the Paramount Skydance bid.”

In addition to the billions Paramount already holds in debt, the company is also set to assume the approximately $33 billion in debt Warner Bros. Discovery holds under the agreement. The deal will be backed by a $54 billion debt commitment from Bank of America, Merrill Lynch, Citi, and Apollo Global Management, as well as $45.7 billion in equity from Larry Ellison.

Regulatory hurdles and other concerns 

In addition to the assumption of substantial debt posing a significant financial burden, Paramount faced several other hurdles in its deal with WBD. 

For one, Ellison has warned about significant job reductions that are expected in the near future. There have already been widespread concerns among critics about potential job losses and lower wages.

Ellison is also a controversial figure in the industry, and his ownership of CBS News has been seen as sympathetic and supportive of the administration of Donald Trump, of whom his father, Larry Ellison, is a major donor. Under Ellison’s ownership of Paramount, reporting critical of the administration has been shelved or received increased scrutiny from Ellison or his appointed head of CBS News, the conservative provocateur Bari Weiss.

This has led to some concern among employees at Warner-owned CNN. Trump has personally sought concessions from news divisions critical of him, including a $16 million settlement from CBS, before his FCC would approve the Ellison takeover of Paramount. Before Netflix bowed out of the deal, Trump pressured the company to fire the former Biden White House official Susan Rice from its board. He has publicly stated his intentions to bring CNN to heel under new owners.

Regulatory scrutiny was another hurdle. Such a large-scale merger attracted attention from lawmakers.

For instance, California attorney general Rob Bonta said in a statement on February 26 that “these two Hollywood titans have not cleared regulatory scrutiny — the California Department of Justice has an open investigation, and we intend to be vigorous in our review.”

A day before Netflix backed out, a coalition of 11 state attorneys general urged the U.S. Department of Justice to review the merger under concerns it will stifle competition and increase subscription prices. This comes months after U.S. senators Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders, and Richard Blumenthal voiced their concerns to the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division, warning that such a massive merger could have serious consequences for consumers and the industry at large. The senators argue that the merger could give the new media giant excessive market power, enabling it to raise prices for consumers and stifle competition.

Despite the DOJ approving the deal in June, a coalition of 12 state attorneys general filed a lawsuit on July 13 to block the merger. The suit argues it would lessen competition and harm movie theaters, cable distributors, and viewers. The coalition is led by Bonta, with Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, and Washington also joining. 

In response, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín issued a 14-day pause. 

What now?

As of October 6, Paramount and Warner Bros. has officially been renamed Skydance, and the new combined corporation will have annual revenue of almost $70 billion. 

In terms of its streaming services— Paramount+, HBO Max, and Discovery+,— those are all set to be combined eventually.

WhatsApp’s rollout of Liquid Glass across its interface continues, with the app now bringing the new look to its video player. Here are the details.

WhatsApp’s slow Liquid Glass rollout continues

Following its initial testing of the Liquid Glass redesign in October 2025, WhatsApp went on to officially release the new look only in May 2026, after months of very limited availability.

Even still, the redesign hasn’t reached everyone, as many 9to5Mac readers continue to report seeing the old interface on their devices.

title: Most US Adults Aren’t Ready for AI to Help With Holiday Shopping, Survey Finds
snippet: Far more people than last year are willing to use AI to help them find the right gift, but few want a bot handling their payment details.
fullText:
AI has the power to be your personal shopping assistant — whether it’s sifting through products to narrow down the right one, tracking the best deals and even ordering items for you without your approval.

But are you really comfortable letting the bots help with your holiday shopping? A recent YouGov survey looked at how US adults feel about it. The results aren’t quite surprising. 

Less than half of Black Friday and Cyber Monday shoppers plan to use AI to help them with holiday shopping. But there’s been some growth since last year. YouGov found that planned AI use has more than doubled within the past year to help navigate sales — from 16% to 34%. 

			

More from CNET

Last year, 21% of holiday shoppers used AI to shop during sales. This year, most of those shoppers (92%) plan to maintain their use of AI or even use it more this year. Only 8% of shoppers who used AI last year plan to scale back on usage this year. But there’s still resistance and hesitancy. Over 4 in 10 (47%) didn’t use AI to shop last year and don’t plan to start this year. Only 22% plan to start this year. What’s the cause for pause?

Most US adults haven’t let AI help them shop yet, but some are considering it

From a global perspective, the US lags behind other countries that use AI tools to help people shop. Over half of adults in Saudi Arabia (54%) and half of adults in India have, while only 18% of adults in the US have. Another 21% said they haven’t yet, but said they would consider doing so. 

That percentage is even higher for Black Friday shoppers, with 30% having already used AI for shopping and 27% considering it.

The divide is stark, however, with 40% of US adults saying they won’t consider using AI for holiday shopping. That’s especially true the further shoppers get into the buying process.

Most shoppers don’t trust AI to make purchases for them

YouGov found that AI is used mostly for discovery when shopping — finding, researching and comparing items. But most shoppers set boundaries the closer they get to checkout. 

Among Black Friday shoppers, 43% say they’re comfortable using AI to find the best deal, while 37% say they’ll use AI tools to track price changes, and 34% compare similar products or offers. But those percentages decline sharply when it’s time to make the purchase. Only 9% would feel comfortable having AI add items to their cart, and 5% would be OK letting AI complete an approved purchase. Only 4% would let it make a purchase without asking. 

Holiday sales aside, AI shoppers are concerned about AI having inaccurate or outdated information (56%), while 51% are concerned about biased or sponsored recommendations. The idea that AI-directed shopping results will steer buyers toward what an advertiser wants, rather than the best deal, may have marketers salivating, but it should give consumers significant pause.

Should you let AI help you shop for the holidays? 

That answer depends on your level of comfort. We know that AI bots can go rogue, share your personal data on the cloud and even spew misinformation. 

I share the same sentiments as many shoppers in the survey. AI has the power to help you narrow down alternatives and find gifts you may not have considered before. It even helped me find a foosball table for my son that I didn’t know existed. But AI hasn’t quite earned my trust to access my payment data, shipping address and other personal details, which could mean big trouble if that data falls into the wrong hands. 

To protect your data, avoid sharing personal details when shopping this season. For instance, simply asking about gifts for a child who loves soccer is enough. There’s no need to share ages or skill levels. You can parse through what’s appropriate yourself.

And double-check any information the bots share — whether it’s deals, product details or, especially, prices. AI tools can be pretty opaque, and you don’t know if you’re actually getting a good deal. Or you may choose to enjoy shopping and perusing deals on your own without the bot’s help to avoid the risks altogether. But if you do decide to enlist AI for automated help, be smart about it.

title: Report: Apple cuts iPhone 18 Pro production due to ‘soft demand’
snippet: Apple has reportedly cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” A new report from Nikkei Asia says Apple has told select suppliers to cut component production for the devices, as price increases allegedly “dampened consumer demand.” more…
fullText:
Apple has reportedly cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” A new report from Nikkei Asia says Apple has told select suppliers to cut component production for the devices, as price increases allegedly “dampened consumer demand.”

Price hikes reportedly dampen iPhone 18 Pro demand

The report cites “multiple familiar with the matter,” and claims Apple has “turned more conservative on shipments since early September. Two of those sources claim that component orders for October have been cut by “at least 15%” compared to what Apple originally requested.

“In October alone, we are seeing orders from Apple reducing by 15% to 20% for both the premium models; we don’t know how things would develop from here,” said one of the executive-level sources. The order cuts will affect production volumes for some, but not all, suppliers in October due to differing production lead times, and it is not immediately clear whether Apple will make further adjustments from November onward.

Another anonymous supply chain manager told Nikkei Asia that demand is “not as strong as previous years when all the new models are introduced all together.” This, of course, refers to Apple not releasing the base iPhone 18 until next spring. Still, the suppliers say that this alone doesn’t account for the lower demand. 

	

One source added that they expect a “similar fate for the iPhone Duo” after it’s released, referring to potential production cuts.

Apple increased prices for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max by $100 compared to their predecessors. While hampering demand, this also means that the impact of that lower demand won’t “immediately translate to lower revenue for Apple,” the report explains.

Apple will report its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings on Monday, November 6. This will provide a look at the first several weeks of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max demand.

title: The investor’s guide to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Everything you need to know
snippet: Year after year, investors who've explored the Expo Halls, met founders, and learned from peers have proven why you need to be on the ground at Disrupt Oct. 13.
fullText:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is built around one question for founders: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era? For investors, it’s the opposite: How do you find that company before someone else does?

At Disrupt, the volume and competition are the point for investors, not a drawback. Year after year, investors who’ve explored the Expo Halls, met founders, and learned from peers at panels and Side Events have proven why you need to be on the ground to get ahead of the curve.

Consider that every founder pitching during the Startup Battlefield competition does so in front of a packed room of VCs. Why? Because they know their next cohort could be sitting right there. All it takes is making the trip to San Francisco this October 13-15.

This guide is for the investors who recognize that three days spent at Moscone West are well worth it and who plan to walk away with the insights and prospects that yield returns.  

And speaking of returns, we have up to $100 in savings with our current ticket tiers, which end Monday, October 12 at 11:59 p.m. PT, so act swiftly to get an even greater ROI on Disrupt. And if you’ve recently been laid off, we have a $75 Expo+ Pass offer to help you make more connections to find your next opportunity.

Let’s dive in!

How Disrupt works for different investors 

Disrupt features numerous tracks, depending on the check sizes you’re able to write and the stage of startup you specialize in.

Angel, pre-seed, scout

If you’re coming to build out your portfolio of early bets and get in on rounds before they’re priced, prioritize the Startup Battlefield 200 semifinalist pitches, the Builders Stage, and the Expo Hall.

Seed, Series A

Disrupt will be all about volume and speed of qualified deal flow. Prioritize the founder list, our curated 1:1 meetings, and the Deal Flow Café. 

Growth, late stage

This stage is best suited for those coming to the event as much for market intelligence and strategic partnership scouting as for deal sourcing. Prioritize the Smart Money and Smart Systems Stages, as well as the exclusive StrictlyVC investor-only session.

Why Disrupt? 

More than 20,000 curated meetings take place over just three days, within dedicated environments like investor receptions and structured networking sessions. Investor-founder connections aren’t hallway luck –they’re built into Disrupt’s infrastructure.

You get direct access to 200 pitch-ready, TechCrunch-vetted startups through Startup Battlefield 200. And we’ll put an emphasis on “vetted.” Our Startup Battlefield team, working alongside TechCrunch’s incredibly discerning team of editors and writers, has done a significant amount of diligence for you already.

Past speakers have included investors like Elad Gil and Vinod Khosla, and this year’s lineup puts you in the room with the operators you’re underwriting, too. We’re talking Rivian’s RJ Scaringe, Amazon’s Panos Panay, Replit’s Amjad Masad, and Cerebras’ Andrew Feldman, just for starters.

The Disrupt crowd is your signal. With a mix of 10,000 founders, investors, and operators filling Moscone West, the companies worth knowing will get discovered by someone. This is your chance to make sure it’s you.

Startup Battlefield 200 is a sourcing engine, not just a pitch competition 

Image Credits:Kimberly White / Getty Images

For founders, Startup Battlefield is a visibility engine and a trial by fire. For investors, it’s a filtered shortlist that the TechCrunch team has spent months narrowing down for you.

Consider that:

200 pre-Series A startups, handpicked by our Startup Battlefield and editorial teams and sharpened through the SB 200 program, are competing for $100,000 in equity-free funding. 

Battlefield alumni have collectively raised over $32 billion and produced 250+ exits, which is evidence we produce fundable companies. 

Startup Battlefield is intensely competitive. Thousands of global startups apply, while just 200 make the cut and only a handful reach the finals. That funnel is doing your top-of-pipeline filtering for you before you ever take a meeting. If you’re not circling around these startups, your competitors are.

The exclusive access that an Investor Pass grants 

We have several different passes for Disrupt, and by joining the community via an Investor Pass, you get access to perks like…

The Deal Flow Café

This is a space exclusively for founders and investors, fostering impromptu run-ins with founders actively seeking capital. Grab coffee or a beverage of choice, explore opportunities, and start conversations that can turn into your next deal.

The founder list

You’ll get early access to the full list of Disrupt founders looking for connections with investors. The next addition to your portfolio can be identified before the event even begins, giving you more time to find even more opportunities.

Curated meetings

Through the Disrupt app, you can schedule 1:1 and small-group meetings with founders matching your focus areas, with AI helping match you by mutual interests instead of waiting on fate.

The investors who make the most out of Disrupt don’t leave sourcing to chance — they’ve already scanned the available resources and set up their agendas in advance.

The Disrupt programming that matters most to Investors 

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images

Our editorially curated programming, including all three days of sessions and panels, is available here, stretching across six stages, breakout sessions, roundtables, and Side Events. Here are some of the stages that might be of interest:

The Smart Money Stage: Interested in capital markets, embedded finance, and stablecoins? Everything within the fintech realm, especially within the intersection of AI, is included.

The Smart Systems Stage: It’s all about compute, infrastructure, and energy economics. If you need to build a justification for underwriting AI infrastructure bets, this is the place to start.

The AI Stage and Real World AI Stages: Get market intelligence on where the fastest-growing startups are deploying, not just building.

The Disrupt Stage: This is where operators and CEOs set the narrative your current and future portfolio companies will be measured against.

Is Disrupt 2026 worth it? 

Disrupt’s value isn’t found in the size of the crowd, though that certainly helps. It’s in the potential, the expertise, the value of that crowd and the feedback it gives you. With so much overlapping investor attention, the companies worth knowing are getting found fast — regardless of whether you’re in the room. The cost of attending is a ticket and three days of your time. The cost of not attending is finding out about your next portfolio company from someone else’s term sheet.

Disrupt 2026 logistics for investors 

We’ve gone in depth about the benefits to you, your portfolio, and the opportunities Disrupt offers you. But there are always matters of hotels, expenses, and travel to sort out. Our Disrupt site has the bulk of these issues covered, but to tackle some common questions and pressing opportunities:

Disrupt passes are discounted until October 13, after which we’ll have higher walk-up rates. That means up to $100 discounts on tickets relative to their final prices.

title: Google is ending support for Pixel Watch’s emergency LTE ‘Safety Signal’
snippet: Google launched the Pixel Watch 2 with “Safety Signal” to ensure users could use Emergency SOS and Safety Check without a Bluetooth or cellular signal. Now, those features require a phone or internet connection. more…
fullText:
Google launched the Pixel Watch 2 with “Safety Signal” to ensure users could use Emergency SOS and Safety Check without a Bluetooth or cellular signal. Now, those features require a phone or internet connection.

The Pixel ecosystem offers a few different life-saving features under the Safety app, which works both on the Pixel Watch and Pixel phones. That includes Emergency SOS for quick access to emergency services, and Fall Detection, which alerts others when the person wearing the watch takes a hard fall and might not be able to contact someone themselves. But it needs a connection to work.

	

All of those still worked for Fitbit Premium, and then for Google Health Premium users on the Pixel Watch 2 or 3 LTE models, as long as the watch didn’t have a Bluetooth or cellular plan connected. Safety Signal essentially allowed the Pixel Watch 2 or 3 to connect to LTE services for that emergency situation – a solid reassurance that those features would work without your phone or a carrier plan.

Google says support for Safety Signal will end on December 12, which means that the safety net won’t exist for much longer. Google says users who are subscribed to Google Health Premium will get an email notification letting them know 30 days prior to the final shutdown. Safety Signal will be operational until that transition period is over.

	

Safety Signal was just the fallback connection plan. Google’s existing standalone safety features will still work with another connection method:

Safety Check

Emergency Sharing

Emergency SOS

Fall Detection

Even though this feature only worked for the Pixel Watch 2 and 3, and then only for the LTE models, it’s still a huge loss.

snippet: The CMF Speaker Series are the first portable Bluetooth speakers from the budget-focused brand that Nothing created but is in the process of spinning off into an India-based standalone subsidiary. There are two versions of the CMF Speaker Se … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

The CMF Speaker Series are the first portable Bluetooth speakers from the budget-focused brand that Nothing created but is in the process of spinning off into an India-based standalone subsidiary. As with many of CMF’s products, like the Headphone Pro that launched a year ago, the new speakers deliver affordability alongside unique designs and bright color options that help them stand out from the competition. While the company doesn’t directly cite a grocery store’s dairy aisle as the inspiration for its latest hardware, it’s hard not to look at these and immediately see electronic milk cartons.

There are two versions of the CMF Speaker Series available starting today in white, dark gray, orange, and turquoise color options. The $59 CMF Speaker S is the smaller of the two and features a “custom-tuned” 45mm full-range driver paired with two passive radiators to help boost the presence of low-end frequencies. The larger $109 CMF Speaker M instead features two drivers including a 10W tweeter and a dedicated 25W woofer for improved bass performance and better separation of instruments and singers.

Both speakers offer up to 18 hours of battery life, have an IP68 water and dust resistance rating, and can have their sound profile customized through the Nothing X app. That customizability extends to the design of the CMF Speaker Series, too. The multifunction knob on the front that controls volume and playback and the speaker’s entire front panel, including the vertical flap on top that can be used for hanging, can be easily removed and swapped with an alternate color or a completely different design. CMF plans to release the official design file so modders can 3D print their own unique customizations.

Other features include a dual-device connection for quickly jumping back and forth between two wireless audio sources Bluetooth 6, fast pairing using NFC, Google Fast Pair, or Microsoft Swift Pair, and audio over a USB-C cable. You can also pair two of the Speaker S or two of the Speaker M (you can’t mix and match) for a left-and-right stereo mode, or synchronize the full mix to several other speakers simultaneously, even from other companies, using an Auracast-based party mode.

title: The best CarPlay upgrades to try in iOS 27
snippet: Apple released iOS 27 to everyone a few weeks ago, and it includes several CarPlay changes worth checking out. Here are a few changes I’ve been loving so far. more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27 to everyone a few weeks ago, and it includes several CarPlay changes worth checking out. Here are a few changes I’ve been loving so far.

CarPlay features to try in iOS 27

Siri AI

Siri AI is the flagship feature of iOS 27, and it extends to CarPlay. In fact, I’ve found it to be especially useful via CarPlay. Siri AI can answer questions around your personal context, world knowledge, and much more in iOS 27.

For example, you can ask Siri to find a specific address or location in your email or text messages, then begin routing to that location, all while using just your voice.

Robust, hands-free control is important in the car, and iOS 27 finally gives Siri the power that it deserves in CarPlay.

Now Playing changes

CarPlay in iOS 27 offers a persistent “Now Playing” MiniPlayer throughout audio apps. This appears in the upper-right corner of the interface and shows playback controls and album artwork.

The Now Playing interface in CarPlay has also been updated to include an audio scrubber at long last. You can drag the scrubber to easily skip to different parts of a song or podcast without using steering wheel controls or reaching for your iPhone.

New wallpapers

CarPlay isn’t known for its robust collection of wallpapers, and Apple doesn’t let you use your own photos for some reason.

In iOS 27, Apple has at least added a collection of new wallpapers that you can choose from. They are similar to the stock iOS 27 wallpapers available on iPhone.

Stability improvements

iOS 27 focuses a lot on platform improvements to performance and reliability, and that applies to CarPlay too. Apple says iOS 27 addresses two key things in CarPlay:

Improved navigation heading and GPS accuracy in CarPlay

Improved wireless CarPlay reliability

So if you’ve ever had problems with those two things in CarPlay, it’s possible that iOS 27 makes the experience much better.

Coming soon(ish): Video app support

Finally, Apple says that developers can now make dedicated video apps for CarPlay in iOS 27. The feature, however, requires support from automakers. This means it might be a while before you can actually use any video apps with CarPlay in your vehicle.

Wrap up

While the dream for many people is still CarPlay Ultra, it’s really nice to see Apple make meaningful improvements to the version of CarPlay already available in millions of cars on the road today.

Have you updated to iOS 27? What CarPlay changes have you noticed? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Google’s Fitbit Air is getting a shiny new Metal Mesh band and better automatic tracking
snippet: The Fitbit Air is finally getting another band option that isn’t fabric or polyurethane. Instead, the Metal Mesh band might actually take the Fitbit Air up a notch. more…
fullText:
The Fitbit Air is finally getting another band option that isn’t fabric or polyurethane. Instead, the Metal Mesh band might actually take the Fitbit Air up a notch.

Band selection for the Fitbit Air has been limited. The Elevated Modern band and Performance Loop options are good, but they lack a little flair. The Fitbit Air needed another band option to take advantage of just how easy it is to swap styles.

The Metal Mesh band fills that gap. It comes in Polished Silver and Champagne Gold with the intent of matching your existing jewelry. The look lets the wearable blend in with an elevated outfit, even if the Performance Loop band does a good job fitting most looks.

Google says the Metal Mesh band for the Fitbit Air will be priced at $69.99. You’ll also be able to buy the Fitbit Air with the Metal Mesh band and the Performance Loop band for $149.99 as a bundle, but it only comes in gold. That’s $20 more than the special editions, like the Steph Curry band and the Pokémon Sleep band, but it comes with two bands instead of a single option.

	

Packed into the band announcement, Google detailed a couple more feature additions to the Fitbit Air, regardless of band choice.

Google announced Health Guardian features that analyze your overall health picture. For Google Health Premium users who set up blood pressure and insulin resistance trends in the app, a report will be available each month to guide lifestyle adjustments. This may give the AI Health Coach some more usability for the average Fitbit user.

Google also notes that automatic activity tracking is getting an overhaul. According to the new post, Google claims the improvements will result in “more intelligent, accurate, and reliable” tracking.

Tracks more activities: We expanded the number of activities your Fitbit tracker or Pixel Watch can detect from 10 to more than 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket and team sports.

Uses more context: Powered by contextual reasoning, Google Health factors in critical context — including your workout routines, historical data, manual edits, and, with permission, your location — to deliver nearly 2x more accurate detections and cut missed workouts by more than half. 7

Logs workouts automatically: Workouts that meet your minimum duration threshold (15 minutes by default) with a sustained elevated heart rate are automatically logged, and a summary is sent to your mobile app, typically within 30 minutes.

Learns your patterns: When you confirm or edit an activity, you’re improving a feature that learns your unique patterns and uses them to refine its predictions.

These updates are planned for “later this month.” This comes as the company recently announced a more expensive $179 tracker called the Fitbit Edge. Unlike the Fitbit Air, this model has a screen carrying Google’s Material You design language.

As for the new Metal Mesh bands, Google has them available for pre-order on its website and at Target. It looks like the new bands should ship later this month.

title: Apple TV’s latest acquisition signals key shift for streamer
snippet: Apple TV just acquired the global streaming rights to Dustfall, a crime series from Australia and the second recent deviation from the streamer’s originals-only strategy. more…
fullText:
Apple TV just acquired the global streaming rights to Dustfall, a crime series from Australia and the second recent deviation from the streamer’s originals-only strategy.

Apple has started licensing more TV series, deviating from all-originals strategy

Ever since Apple TV launched in 2019, it rejected the typical streaming approach of licensing existing content and instead prioritized originals.

Apple has been remarkably consistent with its originals-only strategy. Until recently, the only exceptions have been children’s content that complement its originals (like Peanuts holiday specials), and limited-time bonus films.

But that changed this week, when acclaimed comedy Small Prophets premiered after Apple acquired the rights to the British breakout hit over the summer.

Small Prophets seems like a savvy acquisition. Early reviews call it a “masterpiece” and perhaps “the finest show to hit Apple this year.”

Now today, Apple has announced a second acquisition. Dustfall, an Anna Torv-starring crime series that originated in Australia, will join the streamer in 2027.

Like Small Prophets, Dustfall was created by an international production company and will air in select territories overseas before its global Apple TV premiere.

Clearly, Apple sees acquisitions differently than it once did.

While the streamer isn’t abandoning its successful original-first approach, licensing high-quality series from around the world to beef up its catalog is very much a strategic shift.

And it’s one I’m curious if we’ll see accelerate moving forward.

What do you think of Apple TV licensing third-party series? Let us know in the comments.

Milepost turns your roadtrips into more of a journey. It lets you record all of your drives, and journal all of the key moments that happened along the route, so your roadtrips become a lot more memorable – rather than just a blip of time.

Top features

Most people drive a ton, but a lot of the experience is forgotten once you reach the destination. Milepost helps you keep track of that, by letting you save the route, distance, speed, time, and weather. You can also take notes, add photos, and make it into a true gallery, which the app calls roadbooks. The roadbook serves as a true timeline of your journey, and you can even tie in Apple Music to see what you were listening to while driving.

Milepost isn’t just about your own drives though, it’s also meant to be a social experience. You can share your journeys with friends with its built in social network, and they can also comment and react to what you share. The app supports Siri, Shortcuts, as well as CarPlay. It’s available on all Apple platforms, including the Mac, where you have a larger view to get a more detailed look at your drive. Beyond that, it also offers an MCP server so you can plan future trips with your agents based on what you’ve done in the past.

Milepost is available for free on the App Store for the core experience, but if you subscribe to Milepost Pro, you unlock full drive history, the ability to share more designs, alternative app icons, as well as driving insights. title: New MacBook Pro leak could be very good news for ‘pro’ users
snippet: Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro is coming soon, and the latest leak offers potentially great news for truly ‘pro’ users worried about the rumored thinner design. more…
fullText:
Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro is coming soon, and the latest leak offers potentially great news for truly ‘pro’ users worried about the rumored thinner design.

Redesigned MacBook Pro will be much lighter, but not ‘significantly thinner,’ per Mark Gurman

The MacBook Pro has long attracted customers who may not be ‘pros’ in the sense of doing professional coding work, video editing, photography, or other tasks that require extra computing power.

Plenty of people want a MacBook Pro simply because it’s the best laptop Apple sells. It has the best display in a Mac, the most power, and the longest battery life.

But a new MacBook Pro design is coming, and previous reporting has said it will be thinner and lighter than the current model. Earlier this week Mark Gurman even said it will be “significantly” lighter.

That might sound great to ‘prosumers’ like myself, but it probably raises alarm bells for true ‘pros.’

Last night in a post on X though, Mark Gurman offered good news:

I don’t think it’ll be significantly thinner in the end

— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 7, 2026

Thinner, but not significantly so, while still offering a big weight reduction, sounds like exactly the right balance that should please most users.

If the new design doesn’t bring a drastic reduction in thickness, that’s good news for at least three reasons. It means the new MacBook Pro should:

Retain all or most of its existing ports

Offer battery life that’s not far off from current models

Have plenty of thermal headroom

Weight is generally a more common complaint than thickness with the current MacBook Pro, so if Apple can make the new MacBook Pro easier to carry, slim it down a bit, and still offer the kind of power and versatility pros need, that sounds like a big win.

title: SpaceX to become ‘major mobile carrier’ in US with Starlink Mobile upgrades
snippet: SpaceX has announced plans to make Starlink Mobile a “major mobile carrier in the US” thanks to two major new developments. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
SpaceX has announced plans to make Starlink Mobile a “major mobile carrier in the US” thanks to two major new developments. Here are the details.

SpaceX announces two milestones toward making Starlink Mobile a full-fledged mobile carrier

Starlink Mobile might soon be a full-fledged mobile carrier option for your iPhone. 

SpaceX announced this week two big developments to accomplish this goal.

A new “nationwide low-band spectrum license portfolio”

FCC approval for Starlink Mobile’s Gen2 constellation application

	

The former is a major milestone in the journey toward Starlink Mobile becoming a genuine alternative to other mobile carriers. From the announcement:

While Starlink Mobile’s global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings. Critically, most existing mobile devices already support this underused band.

Final FCC approval hasn’t been granted yet, but SpaceX anticipates it will be and the company can move forward with deploying “a flexible architecture combining our satellite-to-mobile constellation in space with an advanced terrestrial deployment.”

The FCC has approved, however, the deployment of 15,000 satellites that are optimized for 2 GHz spectrum globally. These V2 Starlink Mobile satellites deliver “more than 100 times” the bandwidth of the current generation, boosting connection speeds globally.

title: Spotify starts rolling out audiobooks to more than 180 markets
snippet: Spotify today announced a global rollout of its audiobooks section, giving users in more than 180 markets access to over 350,000 titles spanning more than 120 languages. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Spotify today announced a global rollout of its audiobooks section, giving users in more than 180 markets access to over 350,000 titles spanning more than 120 languages. Here are the details.

Audiobooks coming to 750+ million Spotify users

Four years after launching audiobooks in the U.S., and following a rather limited expansion into select countries in the years since, Spotify today announced that audiobooks are finally coming to more than 180 markets.

As Spotify explained in a blog post, the rollout begins today and will continue through the end of 2026, expanding audiobook access from 22 markets to more than 180 and making the service available to more than 750 million people worldwide.

Users in newly supported markets will have access to more than 350,000 titles, with additional catalogs available in Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Polish, and other languages.

Access will vary depending on the market. Eligible Premium subscribers in countries including Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Poland, Chile, Norway, Peru, Italy, Spain, and Portugal will get 12 hours of audiobook listening each month as part of their existing subscription.

Spotify is also expanding Audiobooks+, an add-on that gives subscribers additional listening hours each month. The service will serve as the primary way to access audiobooks in markets across Africa and Asia, as well as Argentina.

Users will also be able to purchase individual audiobooks outright, while pricing and availability will vary by market.

The company also announced an update to Page Match, its feature for switching between physical or digital books and their audiobook versions. Users can now scan a book’s ISBN barcode, and then enter a page number to find the corresponding point in the audiobook. Spotify added that the feature now works in more than 30 languages.

Audiobooks+ is also expanding to Student plans in Ireland, Belgium, Austria, and Finland beginning in November. Spotify says the add-on has surpassed 1 million subscribers since launching just over a year ago and now generates more than $100 million in annual recurring revenue.

According to Spotify, monthly audiobook listeners grew nearly 40% over the past year, while total listening hours increased by more than 30%.

title: IDC: Mac shipments drop 11% in Q3 as global PC market slides 20%
snippet: Despite seeing an 11% drop in Mac shipments during Q3 2026, Apple’s market share rose from 8.5% to 9.5%, as the broader market saw shipments plunge 20.1%, according to a new report from IDC. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Despite seeing an 11% drop in Mac shipments during Q3 2026, Apple’s market share rose from 8.5% to 9.5%, as the broader market saw shipments plunge 20.1%, according to a new report from IDC. Here are the details.

Apple outperforms most of the PC market under challenging conditions

IDC today released a report on worldwide PC shipments for Q3 2026, noting that Apple significantly outperformed the broader market despite shipping fewer Macs than a year ago.

According to IDC’s preliminary data, Apple shipped 5.9 million Macs during Q3 2026, down 11.3% from 6.7 million in the year-ago period.

The overall PC market, however, fell much more sharply, with worldwide shipments dropping 20.1% year over year to 62.7 million units.

As a result, Apple’s share of worldwide PC shipments actually increased from 8.5% to 9.5%.

This kept Apple in fourth place, behind Lenovo, which topped the ranking with 14.9 million shipments and a 23.8% share, followed by HP with 10.3 million shipments and a 16.5% share, and Dell with 7.6 million shipments and a 12.1% share.

HP recorded the steepest year-over-year decline among the top five vendors, with shipments falling 30.9%. ASUS, meanwhile, saw the smallest decline, down 8.6% year over year, with 5.5 million shipments and an 8.7% share.

	

Here’s IDC:

Vendors and channels bought inventory earlier in the year ahead of price hikes, pulling demand out of Q3. Combined with continued supply constraints, that left the quarter without its usual seasonal lift and pushed shipments below both Q2 and last year.

Looking ahead, IDC says that “channel concern over high inventory and soft demand at elevated prices could bring promotions in the near term,” adding that “pricing will stay well above year-ago levels.”

The firm also says that the economy has weakened since the previous quarter, which could further reduce demand and “darken the outlook for the remainder of 2026 and into 2027.”

title: Googlebook Glowbar doesn’t have the ‘knock-knock’ Chromebook Pixel battery gesture
snippet: One of the beloved features of Google’s original big push into laptops, the Chromebook Pixel, is getting a revival in Googlebook’s Glowbar, but it very much feels like a hollow version of what came before. more…
fullText:
One of the beloved features of Google’s original big push into laptops, the Chromebook Pixel, is getting a revival in Googlebook’s Glowbar, but it very much feels like a hollow version of what came before.

The original Chromebook Pixel launched in 2013 as the launchpad for ChromeOS. To this day, it remains a pretty incredible piece of hardware design, though it was inherently flawed with a truly atrocious display and a sky-high price tag to boot, not to mention an even more restricted operating system compared to what ChromeOS would eventually morph into. Still, it earned a follow-up in 2015’s Chromebook Pixel which delivered a lot of key upgrades.

Both models included a signature hardware feature in the four-piece “light bar” across the top of the lid. It was mainly a design element to ring in the Chrome connection with the four colors of the Chrome and Google logos. It lived on in the later, yet short-lived Pixel C tablet. 

It also served a somewhat practical purpose, too.

	

When you would plug in a Chromebook Pixel, the light bar would give you a rough idea of how much charge was already in the battery. Beyond that, a fun little “knock-knock” gesture on the lid would tell you the same information, but whenever the laptop was just out. You could tap the lid and get an idea of the battery status without opening it up or plugging it in, which was especially useful in a time where laptop battery was still very much Not Great.

It’s that gesture that’s gone on Googlebook’s Glowbar, which retains the light-up action when you plug it in, but loses the “knock-knock” that really grabbed everyone’s attention when Google first launched it. 

What can the Glowbar do? 

Like Chromebook Pixel, it does light up when you plug the machine into power, showing battery status both when it plugged in and unplugged. Useful! It’s also more granular than it was on that older hardware. The only other function, besides an animation when you close the lid, is interaction with Gemini. I struggle to see the utility in that one given the Glowbar is at the back of the display, but I guess why not?

title: Google Labs announces ‘Playground’ for prompt-based game creation
snippet: Google today announced an “experimental gaming platform” called Playground that lets you “create, play, and share” browser-based games. The goal is to “make game creation more approachable and ignite everyday creativity.” more…
fullText:
Google today announced an “experimental gaming platform” called Playground that lets you “create, play, and share” browser-based games. The goal is to “make game creation more approachable and ignite everyday creativity.”

This Google Labs experiment leverages  Gemini, Nano Banana, and Lyria models with a “custom harness to make game creation more accessible.”

It starts with a chat interface that lets you “direct the game just by typing what you want to build.” You can decide between a 2D or 3D game and specify whether it’s single or multi-player. Google offers starter prompts that you can remix and a guided development experience.

Playground lets you “tweak the physics, rewrite the rules, customize the characters, or overhaul the environment.”

	

Google today also previewed a Unity Spark integration that allows for “robust, professional-level mechanics, high-fidelity 3D capabilities, and the flexibility of the Unity runtime.”

The accessibility of Playground and world-class game-building expertise of Unity provides the building blocks for an ecosystem where users can start with a simple text prompt and eventually grow into building immersive experiences with Unity

These are browser-based games that are playable on phone or laptop. Once you’re done, games can be kept private, shared via link, or published to the Playground Explore gallery for everyone. Titles go through safety (community guideline) screening along with user reporting.

Players can rate games, while there’s support for in-game leaderboards with Play Games profile integration.

Google is rolling out Playground starting in the US. Free users will be able to generate games, with expanded access tied to Google One membership.

Google is all about freshness for fall. In addition to announcing the new Fitbit Edge on Monday, the company also has three new features coming to its Fitbit Air, first released in May.

1. Health Guardian 

There’s Health Guardian, Google’s proactive health and safety tools, available in the Google Health app. It works in the background to monitor your body’s health and wellness signals, provides a monthly summary of your health indicators and trends and sends timely notifications for anything that requires your immediate attention.

		

			

Health Guardian features 

In the free Google Health app, Health Guardian includes irregular heart rhythm notifications and high and low heart rate notifications. With the Pixel Watch 3 and up, you also get loss-of-pulse notifications.

In the Premium version, which costs $10 monthly or $100 yearly, you can access these newer features: insulin resistance levels, blood pressure trends and sleep breathing quality trends. They work with the Pixel Watch 3 and up and the Fitbit Air.

Health Guardian will also come to the new Fitbit Edge, though we don’t have a specific date yet. 

Health Guardian passively tracks your health 24/7. Google

Insulin resistance

Insulin resistance refers to when your body doesn’t respond to insulin the way it should. Produced by your pancreas, insulin regulates your body’s glucose levels, moving glucose from your blood into your cells so that it can be used for energy. 

Google Health’s insulin resistance doesn’t rely on readings from a continuous glucose monitor or lab work. Instead, it uses sensors on the Pixel Watch 3 and up and Fitbit Air to estimate insulin resistance and monitor shifts in your metabolic health. 

Specifically, heart rhythm, sleep quality and daily activity data are tracked to give a user an idea of how efficiently their body absorbs energy from food and manages that energy during their activities. 

Note that insulin resistance isn’t intended to monitor real-time glucose levels, and it isn’t a prescreener for diabetes or diabetes management.

Blood pressure

Blood pressure trends rely on optical and movement sensors, pulse and motion patterns and WavesFM, Google’s own AI foundation model, to measure your pulse’s shape and speed beneath your skin. This lets it estimate blood pressure over a month and give you a summary of your heart patterns. 

However, blood pressure trends aren’t a replacement for a blood pressure monitor, so they shouldn’t be used for blood pressure management or as a prescreener for hypertension. It also isn’t designed for pregnant people.

Sleep breathing quality

For users aged 18 and up, sleep breathing quality tracks your breathing overnight to estimate how consistent and easy your breathing was during sleep. It uses your blood oxygen levels and your device’s heart rate and motion sensors. 

With sleep breathing quality, you’ll see each morning how much of your sleep was spent in optimal breathing. Then, at the end of the month, you’ll receive an assessment showing those trends. 

If you’ve been wanting better workout detection with the Fitbit Air, we have good news. Google

Remember that none of these features are for diagnosing or treating diseases. 

2. Upgraded auto-activity detection

The Fitbit Air’s automatic workout detection has been upgraded to be twice as accurate, with 50% fewer missed detections when compared to the existing version. Its large language model can now better detect your workout type based on movement, your routine, logs and location. 

For instance, it can better detect tennis and other racket sports, trail runs and HIIT. 

When she reviewed the Fitbit Air, one of CNET Principal Writer Vanessa Hand Orellana’s biggest and only criticisms of the device was that it missed low-impact workouts like Pilates, so it’s great to see that the Fitbit team paid attention to consumer feedback when revamping its workout detection. 

3. Metal mesh bands

With the Fitbit Air, you could previously choose either recycled polyester and elastane yarn bands or polyurethane bands. Now, metal mesh bands are available in silver and gold. 

The Fitbit Air’s band is also getting a style-forward makeover. Google

This makes the Air look more like jewelry and less like a fitness device. Perfect for those who prefer more discreet wearables that they can wear in any setting. 

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Anna Gragert
						

						

							Senior Editor, Health and Home

Over the past 12 years, Anna has also written for the LA Times, Elle, Bust Magazine, Dazed, Apartment Therapy, Well+Good and more. At CNET, she's a senior editor on the Healthy Home team, and her coverage includes health, wellness tech, meal kits and home and kitchen tech with a focus on the technology that aims to help us live our healthiest, happiest lives.

title: Fitbit Edge May Be the Sweet Spot for Smartwatch Noncommittals
snippet: Google’s new $179 tracker sits between the screenless Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5, promising some of the best parts of both without fully committing to either.
fullText:
If you’re lukewarm on smartwatches but not minimalist enough to go completely screenless, Google may have found your Goldilocks option.

The new $179 Fitbit Edge, unveiled Monday, sits between the $100 Fitbit Air and $400 Pixel Watch 5 in price, features and form factor. It gives you a color screen, built-in GPS and many of the health sensors you’d expect from a smartwatch, but in a slimmer, lighter package with up to a week of battery life.

The concept isn’t new for Fitbit. Previous trackers like the Inspire and Charge paired a simple screen with Fitbit’s health and fitness tracking while working with both iOS and Android; if anything, the screen-less Fitbit Air was the departure. But it’s been three years since the Charge 6, and Google now has a lot more to pull from across its wearable lineup. The Edge combines some of what I like about the minimalist Air with features that have trickled down from the Pixel Watch 5.

			

More from CNET

Whether that combination hits the sweet spot remains to be seen.

The Fitbit Edge is available for preorder on Monday and goes on sale Oct. 27.

The mini screen 

I’m a big fan of the minimalist Fitbit Air, which hides almost every trace of tech behind sleek bands. Aesthetically, it’s my ideal; practically, not so much. I inevitably glance down expecting to see the time, only to get annoyed at this thing seemingly freeloading on my wrist because all the payoff is in the phone app.

Apparently, I want my cake and to eat it too. That’s where the Edge comes in.

Its 1.34-inch color AMOLED display is 46% larger than the one on the Charge 6 and has an always-on option. There’s also a physical side button for pausing workouts and accessing menus.

The Edge keeps with the same style choices that make the Air and Pixel Watch 5 stand out, and as a lover of all things color, I’m here for it. It comes in Obsidian, Fog, Olive and Canyon combinations, with interchangeable options including a performance loop, magnetic band and metal links. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition that costs an additional $50.

Google

Google also redesigned the interface with tiles that resemble the Pixel Watch UI, including watch faces with complications and quick access to workouts and health metrics. It still runs Fitbit’s own operating system rather than Wear OS, so this isn’t a miniature Pixel Watch as it lacks access to the Play Store and Gemini. But it does mean you can use the Fitbit Edge with the iPhone as well as Android phones.

You can get weather, alarms, timers, media controls and turn-by-turn directions. The Edge can also mirror notifications and incoming calls from your phone and send canned replies to messages on Android.

But there’s no microphone or speaker, so you can’t take calls from your wrist as you would on a smartwatch. There’s also no NFC for Google Wallet or tap-to-pay, an odd omission considering the older Charge 6 had it.

More smartwatch-like health and fitness tracking

The Edge also borrows plenty from the smartwatch side when it comes to health and fitness.

Unlike the Fitbit Air, which relies on your phone for GPS, the Edge has built-in GPS and an altimeter. It also tracks heart rate, blood oxygen and skin temperature and supports ECG readings.

Google says heart-rate tracking is 40% more accurate than on the Charge 6, a claim I’m especially interested in testing against a chest strap once I get the Edge on my wrist.

It tracks more than 50 exercise types and can automatically recognize more than 40. Google says it has also improved automatic detection since launching the Air, including the ability to recognize racquet sports.

During workouts, you can see metrics like pace and heart rate zones on your wrist, which I missed on the Air. The Edge can also broadcast live heart rate data to compatible exercise equipment, so you can see your heart rate on a treadmill or other supported machine.

The Edge comes with three months of Google Health Premium, which costs $10 per month or $100 per year after that. Premium unlocks the AI-powered Google Health Coach and Health Guardian, which measure monthly blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Health Guardian is also coming to the Fitbit Air, but Google hasn’t said when.

Seven-day battery comes with an asterisk

Battery life is one of the Edge’s biggest advantages over a smartwatch.

Google rates it for up to seven days per charge, but there’s a massive caveat. That’s the estimate with the raise to wake setting. If you prefer an always-on display (which I do) then the estimate dwindles down to two days, according to Google. 

Google

For me, the deciding factor may be how quickly raise to wake responds. The entire reason I missed having a screen on the Air was the ability to glance down and instantly see the time. If I’m waiting for a black screen to wake up, I might as well have the Air on and just pull out my phone.

Charging is a mixed bag, too. Five minutes on the charger gets you about a day’s worth of battery, but a full charge takes about 90 minutes. Knowing my charging habits — where I don’t have a lot of downtime to recharge my wearable devices for an hour plus — I don’t need hands-on time to predict that I’ll probably never see this thing at 100%.

The Edge uses the same charger as the Air, and Google says you can move between Fitbit devices and the Pixel Watch without interrupting your health data. I can already envision a scenario where I’d use an Edge most days and swap in the Air when I forgot to charge, or want something less distracting. Whether I’d actually buy two devices to accomplish that is another question.

Fitbit’s first tracker with a user-replaceable battery

The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, making it Fitbit’s first tracker designed with this level of repairability. Google has already moved in this direction with the Pixel Watch 4, which was redesigned without adhesives to make repairs easier. My colleague Katie Collins even replaced its screen herself despite describing herself as an “ambitious amateur.”

The battery on the Fitbit Edge is replaceable. 

Bringing that approach to a smaller, less expensive tracker could help extend its life, especially since batteries inevitably degrade over time. Google says repair options vary by region and recommends self-repair only for people with the technical expertise to do it safely. 

Fitbit Edge: Bottom line 

At $179, the Edge costs nearly twice as much as the Fitbit Air and more than Fitbit’s other entry-level trackers. But compared with the Pixel Watch or Samsung’s Galaxy Watch, the price could feel like a deal if you’re prioritizing fitness features and don’t need other smartwatch features like contactless payments. For people who want GPS, a screen and notifications, and found the Air came up short, that extra money buys a lot. Few trackers this capable sell at this price: The next step up would be something like the $249 Apple Watch SE 3 or the $300 Samsung Galaxy Watch 7.

On paper, that makes the Edge a strong pick for people like me who aren’t ready to choose a smartwatch that’s only able to work with an iPhone or an Android phone. Now I need to find out whether it’s my Goldilocks wearable, or whether I’ll end up back with the smartwatch-and-band combo I once thought was my happy medium

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Vanessa Hand Orellana
						

						

							Principal Writer						
					

											

								

											Vanessa is a lead writer at CNET, reviewing and writing about the latest smartwatches and fitness trackers. She joined the brand first as an on-camera reporter for CNET's Spanish-language site, then moved on to the English side to host and produce some of CNET's videos and YouTube series. When she's not testing out the latest health tech, you can catch her on a hike or trail run with her family.

title: Motorola is rolling out its Android 17 update to more devices
snippet: Motorola is expanding its Android 17 rollout, with the update making its way to many more devices including the Razr Ultra (2026) this week. more…
fullText:
Motorola is expanding its Android 17 rollout, with the update making its way to many more devices including the Razr Ultra (2026) this week. 

Motorola detailed its Android 17 update back in August, but timing details were left unclear. Now it seems to be starting to roll out in the US.

Friend-of-the-site and former (before the site was gutted last week) Managing Editor at Android Central, Derrek Lee, noticed the Android 17 update landing on his Motorola Razr Ultra (2026) this week as a 4.17GB update carrying the version number A171WLH.38-19-5. It’s still based on the September 2026 security update.

Motorola’s condensed changelog notes a “fresh, expressive design” and “smarter notifications,” both of which were detailed in a previous detailed overview of the update. 

	

Interestingly, the update has yet to land for the Motorola Razr Fold at this point, but one would imagine that’s not too far away. 

The Razr Ultra (2026) isn’t the only device being updated, though. The floodgates seem to have opened with Edge 60 Fusion, Edge 60 Pro, Motorola Signature, and more all being updated in the past few days. Edge 70 devices were updated a few weeks ago.

title: Googlebook’s Android-integrated features won’t work with Samsung phones at launch
snippet: Googlebook is pitched as the laptop for Android users but, at launch, the vast majority of Android users can’t use the platform’s best features. more…
fullText:
Googlebook is pitched as the laptop for Android users but, at launch, the vast majority of Android users can’t use the platform’s best features.

Built on top of Android, Googlebook’s core pitch is to be the laptop for Android users, with deep integration between your smartphone and laptop. This includes a host of features such as instant hotspot, notification sync, phone file access, and the ability to continue tasks started on your phone from your Googlebook laptop. You can also stream apps from your phone’s display to your Googlebook directly.

In terms of deep integration, is a good pitch, but it won’t work for a lot of users at launch.

On a support page, Google confirms that Googlebook’s suite of Android integrations won’t work with any device running Android 16 or prior – Android 17 is the minimum requirement. 

	

Beyond that, Google also confirmed that Samsung devices are not supported at launch. Rather, support is rolling out “over the coming weeks.” It’s not mentioned whether Google or Samsung needs to push an update here, but it stands to reason that an update on Samsung’s end might be needed.

Support for Better Together features will be rolling out across all Android 17-supported Samsung devices over the coming weeks. Sorry for the inconvenience!

Meanwhile, Googlebook faces some other early hiccups, such as lacking support for Slack’s web app at launch, a key workplace app, as well as some apparent optimization issues for apps running on Intel hardware.

title: iOS 27.0.1 is now Apple’s recommended update for users still on iOS 26
snippet: Apple launched iOS 27 on September 14, but the new OS version was initially minimized in Settings while iOS 26.7 was spotlighted as the recommended update. But now following the release of iOS 27.0.1, that has officially changed. more…
fullText:
Apple launched iOS 27 on September 14, but the new OS version was initially minimized in Settings while iOS 26.7 was spotlighted as the recommended update. But now following the release of iOS 27.0.1, that has officially changed.

iPhones running iOS 26 will default to iOS 27.0.1 as next update

Over the last few years, Apple has started rolling out its major new iOS updates more gradually.

For example, while iOS 27 officially became available to all users on September 14, it wasn’t featured as the default, top-level update in the Settings app.

Instead, until very recently, users saw iOS 26.7 as the recommended update, while iOS 27 was minimized under a small ‘Also Available’ section in the Software Update screen.

Apple does this because inevitably, despite a months-long beta process, there are often new bugs that emerge following the public launch. And the company wants the chance to address these before pushing the update to its full user base.

But now with iOS 27.0.1 available, Apple has made iOS 27 the default update for users still on iOS 26.

So the next time those users go to Settings ⇾ General ⇾ Software Update, they’ll see iOS 27.0.1 featured prominently.

Users will still have the option of staying on iOS 26. But we can expect to see iOS 27 adoption accelerate now that Apple has made it the primary update in Settings.

Last year Apple waited until after iOS 26.1 was available before recommending the switch from iOS 18. So pushing iOS 27 much earlier this year is a clear endorsement of the company’s focus on bug fixes and stability with its latest major update.

title: Claude launches Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides integration with sidebar and more
snippet: If Gemini isn’t quite your cup of tea, Anthropic’s Claude now supports sidebar integration with Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides. more…
fullText:
If Gemini isn’t quite your cup of tea, Anthropic’s Claude now supports sidebar integration with Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides.

You can already use Gemini natively in Google Workspace apps, but those invested in Claude can now use their AI of choice inside of Google’s ecosystem through the Claude for Google Workspace add-on which is in public beta starting today. A sidebar opens up alongside your file in Docs, Sheets, or Slides and can assist in building out documents, making edits, and more.

In Google Docs, Anthropic says you can use Claude integration to fix spelling, rewrite portions of a document, or restyle sections, all without breaking existing formatting. In Sheets, you can have Claude write formulas or build tables using the context of the document, or even upload extra documents/spreadsheets to build something new in Sheets. In Slides, Claude can build new slides using existing layouts or themes or flag elements that might need to be updated. Gemini can do much of this but, as mentioned, this is useful for those already invested in Claude.

There’s an “ask before edits” mode where Claude will let you preview changes before they’re made.

	

The Claude for Google Workspace beta is available to all paid Claude users through the Google Workspace marketplace. There are also new Claude connectors for Docs, Sheets, and Slides that let you edit Google Workspace files directly from Claude itself just by pasting a file link into your conversation with the AI.

fullText:
Last year, Kuxiu was the first to make chargers that perfectly match the Cosmic Orange iPhone. They released their 3-in-1 X40 turbo and their S4 Solid State battery pack. They both matched the orange color so well that it seemed as if they were 1st-party accessories. This year, the new hero color for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup is burgundy, and Kuxiu is back at it again with a new matching burgundy D5 5-in-1 charging station. With its premium build quality, perfect color matching, built-in cooling, and price, this charger is everything you need from a performance and aesthetic standpoint.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video below!

Kuxiu D5 specs & features

I reviewed their original D5 a few months back, and it was one of my favorite chargers of the year. Now they have brought it all back with some awesome-looking accents and features. The Kuxiu D5 is advertised as a 5-in-1 charger because it charges three devices but also features a built-in cooling fan and a diagnostics display. You get:

Qi2.2 25W wireless charging

Retractable Apple Watch charging puck

AirPods charging mat

Built-in cooling fan that can be manually turned off and on

Smart color display to give us real-time charging stats

Includes 45W charging brick and braided cable in the packaging

While it is not as compact as something like their X40 Turbo, there is still some thought put into portability and travel with this charger. The Qi2.2 charger can fold down flat into a small cube you can take wherever you need, and the Apple Watch charger retracts into the charger as well. For me, it has worked best as a permanent desk charger, but it’s nice to know that it is also portable. 

My experience

As I mentioned, I have been using the original black color for a few months as my main desk charger. It is reliable, functional, and simple to use. So when Kuxiu announced their Burgundy version, I knew I had to check it out, especially since I was looking for some Burgundy color-matching accessories for my new iPhone 18 Pro. 

Since I knew this charger was already great, I wanted to see how closely the color matched the iPhone 18 Pro, and I was impressed by how identical it was. The aluminum parts of the D5 match the Burgundy on the iPhone 18 Pro, and they add other burgundy accents across the charger’s different materials. 

Beyond the aesthetics, my favorite part is the built-in cooling fan because it adds tangible value to the setup. I am someone who constantly installs new iOS betas, tests new features, and puts my phone through situations where it tends to get warm. So, having the active cooling system built directly into the charger has been game-changing in keeping my phone efficiently cooled and helping it sustain 25W charging for longer, since it does not get warm. The fan is also dead silent, but if you do want to turn it off, you can do so with one tap. Then, of course, you have the diagnostics display that shows you all the charging stats you need to see from all the active chargers. 

Pricing & availability

The Kuxiu D5 is available today on Kuxiu’s site in the original Space Grey and their new Burgundy color. You also get the required 45W charging brick and a braided USB-C cable. It is currently on sale for $59.99. 

Final take

For under $60, I challenge someone to find me a high-quality 3-in-1 charger that offers all the features above and includes all the charging accessories you need to use it at its best. That is why Kuxiu is one of the brands I recommend the most; it’s the performance-to-price ratio that sets them apart. So if you just picked up a new Burgundy iPhone or you are in the market for a new 3-in-1 charger, I highly recommend checking this one out. My only wish is that the next version has a USB-C port so you can charge a 4th device, like a smart ring or something. Otherwise, this thing is great.

fullText:
I use iPhone Mirroring every day to quickly access my iPhone directly from my Mac, and it’s even better this year. iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate were released last month, bringing three key updates to iPhone Mirroring. Here’s everything new.

macOS 27: What’s new for iPhone Mirroring 

The biggest change for iPhone Mirroring in macOS 27 is the ability to resize the iPhone Mirroring window.

As my colleague Marcus reported last week, you can now adjust the size of the iPhone Mirroring window with any iOS 27-compatible apps. Right now, that means it only works for Apple’s native iPhone apps. However, once developers start rolling out iOS 27 updates later this year, support for resizing will expand rapidly.

Previously, iPhone Mirroring on macOS only support three preset sizes: smaller, actual size, and larger. The change in macOS 27 Golden Gate and iOS 27 clearly indicates Apple is prepping for the foldable iPhone Ultra, expected to launch later this year.

iPhone Mirroring in macOS 27 and iOS 27 also has several other updates:

Control Center access

DRM video support

Previously, iPhone Mirroring did not support accessing Control Center at all. In macOS 27, you can access it with the CMD+4 keyboard shortcut or with the “View” menu in your Mac’s menu bar.

DRM video support means you can watch protected videos using iPhone Mirroring on your Mac. Previously, all DRM-protected videos would simply show a black screen when iPhone Mirroring was enabled.

macOS 27 also has a new app icon for iPhone Mirroring, just like it does for many other stock Apple apps.

title: Apple planning huge iPhone Duo demo experiences at select retail stores: report
snippet: iPhone Duo is just about two weeks away from releasing, and according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has big retail plans ahead for its first foldable iPhone, to make sure every customer gets to see it to the fullest. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is just about two weeks away from releasing, and according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has big retail plans ahead for its first foldable iPhone, to make sure every customer gets to see it to the fullest.

Apple is gearing up for a major launch with the iPhone Duo, which should be no surprise. What is a surprise though, is the amount of attention Apple is putting into making sure this launch goes as smoothly as possible.

In the newsletter, Gurman reports that the company is planning to have over a hundred demo units at some of its biggest stores:

The company is preparing a major retail push, with a huge number of demo units at its flagship stores. The Fifth Avenue location in New York City is expected to have more than 150 units across hands-on demo stations and in-store fixtures. The Apple Park Visitor Center at the company’s home base, meanwhile, will have nearly 100. Other locations, including Michigan Avenue in Chicago, the Grove in Los Angeles and the Upper West Side in Manhattan, will each have roughly 30 to 40 units.

Some of its smaller stores will only have around 20 units, which still seems bigger than usual, given the fact that there are only two colors. Given how hard it’ll be to buy a Duo at launch, allowing a lot of hands-on demos at once seems sensible.

iPhone Duo demo fixtures

Beyond the number of demo units, the company has also designed a new MagSafe stand that can hold an unfolded iPhone Duo, alongside two “standard” iPhones (likely iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.) There’ll also be iPhone Duo demo units without a security tether “along the sides of stores,” so users can demo StandBy mode and other features.

Lastly, the company is planning a new fixture for some Apple Stores that showcase the iPhone Duo opening and closing, so it’s “impossible to miss” when you walk into an Apple Store.

All in all, iPhone Duo will become the forefront of Apple Stores after its launch on October 23rd. It’ll be hard to get, so if you’re interested in owning one – make sure you’re geared up to preorder it on October 16th.
