title: Apple Home adds two powerful new features in iOS 27
snippet: Apple is launching several new Home products next week, so it’s no surprise that iOS 27 includes big upgrades in the Home app. Here are two powerful new Home features in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
Apple is launching several new Home products next week, so it’s no surprise that iOS 27 includes big upgrades in the Home app. Here are two powerful new Home features in iOS 27.

#1: HomeKit Secure Video packs big upgrades in iOS 27

HomeKit Secure Video is Apple’s secure, cloud-based service included with iCloud+ for compatible video cameras. It lets you record footage, view it from anywhere, and set up activity automations.

In iOS 27, Apple Intelligence powers three new HomeKit Secure Video upgrades (via Apple):

Generated video descriptions: “users can quickly understand what happened across a sequence of video clips, even without watching them.”

Search in clips: “[users] can easily find what they’re looking for, like a package delivery.”

Noteworthy clips: “At the top of the Search page, the Home app elevates noteworthy clips that users may want to review, so they can quickly see important moments.”

Joining these is a fourth feature, not powered by AI, that’s been on users’ wishlists for a while: 4K video. Apple says, “supported HomeKit Secure Video cameras can now stream and record in 4K.” Previously, 1080p was the max resolution.

If you’re looking for a HomeKit Secure Video-compatible camera, I’d recommend:

Aqara G100 2K security camera: Excellent budget-friendly option currently only $33

eufy 4K security camera: For 4K support if you have more to spend

#2: Real-time notification updates

Most of the Home app’s upgrades this year focus on HomeKit Secure Video. But there’s also another AI-powered new feature: real-time updating notifications.

Here’s how Apple describes it:

The Home app draws on Apple Intelligence to understand related notifications as a single activity, so users receive one notification that updates as the activity happens.

Inside a new Apple Intelligence section of the Home app’s settings screen, you’ll see a ‘Reduce Notifications’ toggle. It explains: “Combine related activities, such as someone arriving and unlocking the door, in one notification that updates in real time.”

Essentially, Home app notifications will stop showing outdated information, and only focus on the latest, most relevant info.

So instead of seeing the seven related notifications above, you’ll get one alert that says: ”Lydia arrived. Checked the mail. Garage Door was closed.”

title: Google Find Hub tags adding NFC support, better registration
snippet: According to the latest version of Google Play services, Find Hub tags are getting two new capabilities. more…
fullText:
According to the latest version of Google Play services, Find Hub tags are getting two new capabilities.

Version 26.39 of Google Play services has two Security & Privacy features related to the Find Hub network.

[Phone] With NFC support, you can quickly access Find Hub tag details and settings or identify lost tags when you tap the tag with your phone.

Find Hub devices that support NFC can be tapped with a phone to reveal “details and settings or identify lost tags.” At the moment, you have to place lost tags in an identification mode to get details, with the process varying between products. Tapping would be much easier.

NFC is not a common feature on Find Hub trackers. For example, it’s absent on the upcoming Pixel Tag. The Xiaomi Tag released earlier this year has NFC, but it appears limited to Apple’s Find My network. That said, Play services adding this support suggests such devices are coming.

	

[Phone] With the new registration flow, you can now set categories, rename tags, and configure features like Left-Behind Reminders when you first set up your Find Hub network tags, so you don’t have to configure them manually in the app later.

The second update introduces an improved setup process. It lets you set a category (Bag, Bike, Car, etc.), rename tags, and control other settings when you first register a device. Previously, you had to open the Find Hub app to do all this.

title: Tim Cook sold nearly $63.9 million in Apple shares this month
snippet: Apple executive chair and former CEO Tim Cook sold nearly 200,000 Apple shares on October 2, one day after more than 374,000 restricted stock units vested as part of his compensation package. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple executive chair and former CEO Tim Cook sold nearly 200,000 Apple shares on October 2, one day after more than 374,000 restricted stock units vested as part of his compensation package. Here are the details.

As reported by Investing.com (via MacMagazine), Tim Cook sold 191,753 Apple shares on October 2, following the settlement of 374,541 restricted stock units (RSUs) on October 1.

RSUs are a form of stock-based compensation that entitle an employee to receive company shares once certain conditions are met. In Cook’s case, the number of shares that vested was determined by Apple’s total shareholder return relative to other S&P 500 companies over a three-year period.

According to the filing, Cook’s shares were sold across multiple transactions at prices ranging from $330.66 to $334.50 per share. At the time of publication, Apple stock was trading at $333.84 per share.

The report adds:

Apple withheld 199,038 shares, valued at $65,746,232 based on a price of $330.32 per share, to cover tax withholding requirements related to the RSU vesting.

Investing.com notes that the sale was carried out under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan that Cook adopted in May, meaning the transaction had been arranged in advance rather than decided on the day of the sale.

Cook also transferred 26,325 Apple shares as a gift on October 2, although the filing does not identify the recipient.

Even after the sale, the tax withholding, and the gifted shares, Cook still holds more than 3.2 million Apple shares through his trust.

title: Where Google Wallet state IDs are available on Android
snippet: States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android. more…
fullText:
States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android.

Update 10/10

How to add your state ID on Android

Open the Google Wallet app on Android 9+

Tap the “plus” button next to “View more” at the bottom

Choose “ID & personal info” and then “Driver’s license or state ID” 

Select your state and follow the instructions

The process involves taking a picture of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of yourself for verification: a “photo from this video will be submitted to your ID issuer.” 

Once approved, the ID will appear below the carousel of payment methods alongside other passes. The order can be rearranged, while you can remotely remove the ID online if your phone is missing: myaccount.google.com > Personal Info > Manage IDs.

	

Related: Google Wallet rolling out stacked card list redesign on Android

What Google Wallet state IDs are supported

Arizona (Rolled out October 2023)

Arkansas (Rolled out October 2025)

California (Rolled out August 2024)

Colorado (Rolled out October 2023)

Georgia (Rolled out October 2023)

Iowa (Rolled out June 2025)

Maryland (Rolled out December 2022)

Montana (Rolled out August 2025)

New Mexico (Rolled out December 2024)

North Dakota (Rolled out October 2025)

Ohio (Rolled out September 2026)

[New] Oklahoma (Rolled out October 2026)

Puerto Rico (Rolled out October 2025)

Where state IDs are coming next

Google previously said to expect support in the following places:

West Virginia (Upcoming availability announced April 2025)

Where you can use state IDs

The primary place you can use this digital ID is at TSA checkpoints in some US airports. There are two ways to do so, starting with tapping your phone at the NFC terminal. You then review the information that will be shared with the TSA and authenticate with device unlock. There’s also a QR code method that requires opening the ID in Google Wallet. 

Officially, you still have to carry the physical ID card at all times.

Some apps, like from car rental services, are beginning to accept digital IDs for identity and age verification. On mobile, if an app or website requests your age, it’s as simple as confirming (and authenticating) that you want to share this information with a system-level prompt/sheet. On desktop web, the experience involves scanning a QR code. 

Google wants to make it possible to do that “without any possibility to link back to a user’s personal identity” through what it calls Zero-Knowledge Proof. This technology will be open-sourced for anyone to use. 

Looking ahead, the IDs can be used at DMVs in Arizona, Georgia, Maryland, and New Mexico as part of “improved and streamlined customer experiences.”

	

Google is also working on letting you use digital IDs to “recover Amazon accounts, access online health services with CVS and MyChart by Epic, verify profiles on platforms like Uber and more.”

Using passport as REAL ID

Google in April pointed out how you can “use your ID pass created from a U.S. passport with TSA security for domestic travel at supported airports, even if you do not have a REAL ID driver’s license or state-issued ID.” This comes ahead of the May 7, 2025 deadline. 

To do so, open Google Wallet > Add to Wallet > ID pass. This three-step process involves taking a picture of your passport’s info page, and then scanning the security chip found inside the back cover of your passport. You also have to record a video of your face that Google will review “to make sure you’re a real person, and compare the video to your passport photo to make sure you’re the owner of the passport.”

The NFC and QR code instructions for using this digital passport ID are unchanged from above. You also have to keep the physical version on you when traveling. As a reminder, this won’t work internationally.

title: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablet finally gives the iPad lineup some much needed competition
snippet: This week, Amazon unveiled a new lineup of Alexa Tablets. They no longer run a proprietary OS with a custom App Store, and instead embrace Android with a stock feel – while offering the Play Store. It’s a big shift in direction for Amazon. The tablets also look quite beautiful, while previous Fire tablets have felt cheap. I think these have the opportunity to do quite well. more…
fullText:
This week, Amazon unveiled a new lineup of Alexa Tablets. They no longer run a proprietary OS with a custom App Store, and instead embrace Android with a stock feel – while offering the Play Store. It’s a big shift in direction for Amazon. The tablets also look quite beautiful, while previous Fire tablets have felt cheap. I think these have the opportunity to do quite well.

First and foremost, I want to make it quite clear that I’m not saying the iPad is doomed or anything remotely close to that. However, I do think the Alexa Tablet serves as a real form of iPad competition, which the iPad has generally lacked.

New Alexa tablets serve as strong competition

Amazon is putting a lot of care into these tablets that other Android manufacturers haven’t, and while these tablets come in at lower price points – they certainly punch above their weight class.

There are three Alexa Tablets to start off the lineup: an 8.7” model at $229, an 11” model at $329, and a 12” Pro model at $499. To me, the one in the middle is the most interesting.

It offers 8GB of RAM, a 90Hz display, a thin design, and a similarly sharp display. That compares to the budget iPad, which comes in $120 higher with less RAM, a lesser display, and a thicker design. Granted, the iPad has the A16 chip, which probably feels much faster than the MediaTek chip powering it. The iPad also starts at 128GB, compared to the 64GB on the Alexa Tablet. Once you upgrade the Alexa Tablet to 128GB, there’s only a $70 difference.

Hardware wise, the Alexa Tablets seem pretty competent. Obviously, Android on tablets isn’t going to be quite perfect, but given its tie in with Alexa and the fact that the tablet is priced quite well, I could see a lot of people wanting to buy these, even if they potentially would’ve considered iPads. Of course, one strong suit from Amazon is the Kindle experience, and these Alexa Tablets offer a reader mode that cuts blue light.

Wrap up

Only time will tell, but Amazon might make a pretty big dent into the tablet market with its new entries. Even the 12” Pro at $499 seems like a really worthwhile product. At the very least, I hope some strong competition means Apple will be less complacent with its iPad upgrades. For example, the iPad Air has largely only received chip upgrades since its last redesign in 2020.

	

I’m personally excited to try one of these out and truly put it to the test. Right now, Amazon also offers 20% off with any trade-in, making it an even better deal.

What do you think of these new Alexa Tablets? Would you consider getting one of these for a friend or family member during the holiday season? Sound off in the comments.

title: TechCrunch Mobility: A roadblock clears for self-driving trucks
snippet: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
fullText:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

I’m back from a sojourn through New Hampshire’s White Mountains — a few days of respite before Disrupt 2026, TechCrunch’s annual tech conference in San Francisco. Now, after a few days immersed in fall colors, I am ready for the action. And there is gonna be a lot of it. 

I want to see you all there, so here is a 30% discount on tickets to Disrupt with code mobility30. For more info on the show, scroll down.

Now, on to the news!

Self-driving truck companies Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI received a federal exemption this week that removes a massive barrier to commercialization. 

Under federal regulations, if a traditional big rig runs into trouble, the human driver must pull over, activate the hazard lights, and then physically place reflective warning triangles on the road within 10 minutes to alert other road users. But if a mechanical problem forces a self-driving truck to pull over, there’s no human driver to deploy those warning devices.

It was a big enough hurdle that Aurora took federal safety regulators to court over the requirement. After the court denied its request for an exemption, the company escalated the fight to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Companies did have a temporary waiver as it awaited a decision.)

Now Aurora and other self-driving truck developers have been given the green light from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. The agency has granted a five-year exemption allowing companies to replace roadside warning devices, such as reflective warning triangles, with cab-mounted warning beacons. Check out Aurora’s first responders page to see how it works.

Image Credits:Aurora Innovation

Daniel Goff, vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, said the exemption will help the industry “usher in an autonomous era of freight movement on U.S. roads, one that can save lives and improve the efficiency of goods delivery.”

Gerardo Interiano, Aurora’s head of government relations and public affairs, echoed that sentiment, saying the decision underscores the government’s recognition of the economic and community benefits of autonomous trucking. He described the high-visibility, cab-mounted warning beacons as a “critical, 21st-century solution that enhances roadside safety by immediately alerting other road users without ever needing to put a person in harm’s way.”

One question I’m left with: Could these cab-mounted warning beacons eventually become standard equipment across the entire trucking industry?

A little bird

Image Credits:Bryce Durbin

It’s been a few months since Redwood Materials, the battery-recycling company started by Tesla co-founder JB Straubel, kicked off a restructuring to focus more on energy storage. The first stage of the restructuring involved laying off around 135 employees, or 10% of its workforce.

But a little bird recently told us that some more executives were on their way out the door. Sure enough, over the last few weeks, Redwood’s vice presidents of engineering, operations, treasury, and external affairs have all left the startup.

Got a tip for us? Email Kirsten Korosec at [email protected] or my Signal at kkorosec.07, or email Sean O’Kane at [email protected]. 

Deals!

Image Credits:Bryce Durbin

Waymo has relied on capital from its parent company Alphabet and high-profile venture firms to fund its autonomous vehicle tech plans. This week, the company turned to debt financing for the first time for another bump. A $5 billion bump to be exact. 

PIMCO, Blackstone, and Sixth Street were the lead lenders. But there were so many more, including Capital Group, Loomis Sayles, T. Rowe Price, Apollo, Blue Owl, Diameter Capital Partners, Franklin Templeton, Fidelity Management & Research Company, HPS Investment Partners, and Oaktree.

The debt financing comes as the company accelerates its commercial expansion within existing cities while pushing into new markets in the United States, Europe, and Japan. 

Other deals that got my attention this week …

Bloom has raised $3.6 million to become the “Alibaba” of American manufacturing. The seed round was led by SNAK Venture Partners and included Flyover Capital, deep tech firm Mana Ventures, Detroit Venture Partners, Invest Detroit Ventures, and the Michigan Outdoor Innovation Fund.

Flai, a startup that developed AI software for dealerships, raised $27 million in a Series A funding round led by automation-focused firm Base10 Partners. The round included funding from dealers (Friedkin Group and Findlay Automotive), Toyota’s venture arm, Y Combinator, and First Round Capital.

Parallel Systems, a startup developing a rail vehicle capable of moving over several tons of freight as far as 500 miles without an operator, raised $100 million in a Series C round led by AVP, with participation from Hillspire, Agility Global, Cobalt Capital, Anthos Capital, Congruent Ventures, Riot Ventures, and Collaborative Fund. 

Uber has agreed to buy catering company ezCater in an all-cash transaction valued at $2.3 billion.

Notable reads and other tidbits

Image Credits:Bryce Durbin

Surveillance camera maker Flock cut its workforce by 18%, or around 270 employees, as the company faces ongoing and growing backlash to its license plate readers and people-tracking technology. FYI:  Flock founder and CEO Garrett Langley will be at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. 

Lucid Motors built 2,954 electric vehicles in the third quarter of this year, a 54% drop from a year ago, as the company purposely limits production to better meet demand for its EVs.

Kodiak AI has a new 435-mile autonomous route between Dallas and Laredo, Texas, with carrier Charger USA. The self-driving trucks startup is hauling refrigerated and dry freight for consumer packaged goods and for food and beverage customers.

Tesla changed the name of its advanced driver assistance system in Europe after pushback from Germany’s transportation ministry. It’s now called “Tesla Assisted Driving” instead of “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”

Uber and Chinese autonomous vehicle maker Pony.ai plan to launch a robotaxi service in London as part of an expanded partnership to bring driverless cars to Europe.

One more thing

Here’s a bit more info on TechCrunch Disrupt 2026!

I will kick off the conference on October 13 with Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe. Senior reporter Sean O’Kane has a fireside interview with Agility Robotics CTO Jonathan Hurst, as well as a panel featuring Also CEO Chris Yu, General Catalyst’s Yuri Sagalov, and Shan Shan, investment manager at Baillie Gifford. 

I will also interview Shield AI CTO Nathan Michael; Waabi founder and CEO Raquel Urtasun; and Mikell Taylor, director of robotics strategy at GM about building AI systems when failure isn’t an option. And I will interview Foxglove CEO Adrian MacNeil and Bedrock Robotics CTO Kevin Peterson about taking physical AI from prototype to product. 

Not enough? OK, here ya go: We will also have Max Hodak, co-founder of Neuralink and founder of Science Corp.; Ricursive Intelligence co-founders Dr. Anna Goldie and Dr. Azalia Mirhoseini; Hello Robot co-founder and CEO Aaron Edsinger and their robot Stretch 4; and Mark Wahlberg. Plus, hear from engineers and execs from Anthropic, Gamma, Hugging Face, OpenAI, Nvidia, and Replit, as well as investors from Google Ventures, Greylock, Eclipse, Index Ventures, NEA, and Upfront Ventures (to name a few.)

Check out the agenda here.

title: watchOS 27 adds three new apps to your Apple Watch
snippet: watchOS 27 is the latest major software update for Apple Watch, and among its variety of new features, it adds three new apps to your Watch. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27 is the latest major software update for Apple Watch, and among its variety of new features, it adds three new apps to your Watch.

#1: Siri

Siri just got a major AI overhaul in watchOS 27, and one part of that is a brand new Siri app.

The Siri app is available across iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Vision Pro, and also the Apple Watch.

watchOS 27 still lets you invoke Siri via the Digital Crown, but the app is another place you can go to start a conversation. Perhaps more importantly, the app is where you can browse past ones.

Siri AI is more conversational than the old assistant, and keeps a record of past queries across all your devices. So the Siri app in watchOS 27 shows you conversations not just from your Apple Watch, but from your iPhone, Mac, and more.

#2: Find My

Joining iOS 27’s new features for the Find My app, Apple has rethought the Find My experience in watchOS this year too.

In watchOS 26, Find My was split up into three separate apps: Find Devices, Find Items, and Find People.

But in watchOS 27, Apple has streamlined all finding features into a new, unified ‘Find My’ app.

Find My on Apple Watch provides all the functionality of the previous three apps, but in a condensed experience so you can easily locate anything or anyone on a map-centric view.

You can switch between different things you’re looking for via a menu in the top-left corner, but otherwise you’ll see a consistent interface.

#3: Readiness

If you own an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, watchOS 27 also adds a third app: Readiness.

Here’s what the Readiness app does, per the App Store:

The Readiness app analyzes your recent activity, vitals, and sleep to help you understand your capacity to take on the day.

Features

Get a score and a clear classification of your readiness, including Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It.

See an explanation of relevant factors and tap through to associated apps.

Add complications and Smart Stack widgets for convenient and glanceable insights.

View additional details in the Fitness app on iPhone.

Essentially, Readiness provides you a quick glimpse into your overall vitals so you know how well rested and ready your body may be on a given day.

title: Google Docs and Drive now support markdown files natively
snippet: Spurred by the use of markdown files in the AI age, Google Drive and Google Docs are adding full, native support for markdown (.md) files. more…
fullText:
Spurred by the use of markdown files in the AI age, Google Drive and Google Docs are adding full, native support for markdown (.md) files.

Google has been building out markdown support in Drive for years now, but prior steps largely included converting markdown into a format that Docs could use.

Now, Google Drive and its suite of apps can open, edit, and fully use markdown files throughout Docs and other apps. This includes real-time editing and comments with full rendering of the formatting of markdown documents. Google also points out that this benefits AI use cases such as having AI agents collaborate on documents and even syncing with Gemini Notebook.

Google explains:

	

Now that users can handle markdown files natively in Google Docs, they can open, edit, and collaborate on markdown files without changing the file type. Editing Markdown files in Docs also enables both users and agents to collaborate without forcing anyone to write raw syntax, handle manual file conversions, or give up Docs’ real-time editing and commenting tools.

Drive also now supports rendered markdown, so you can view fully formatted, beautiful documents with clickable links and structured tables right in Drive.

Google’s Chandu Thota calls out that markdown “has become the common language between humans and AI agents.”

Markdown support in Google Drive and Docs is rolling out starting today but may take up to 15 days to show up for everyone. It’s enabled by default, even on admin-controlled accounts.

title: Android is the best and worst thing about Googlebooks
snippet: I’ve been testing two Googlebooks: this Asus model, and HP’s too. My first week with the new Android-powered laptops has been about as rocky as anyone's, but I've slowly learned to like them, even if love still feels a ways off. Every moment that's impressed me has been thanks to Android, whether I've been accessing a native version of a useful app or quickly checking my phone notifications from the laptop user interface. But man, sometimes it just sucks. Phone connectivity is flaky, app casting is awkward, and file-sharing seems to be flat-out broken. And that's just the interaction between a Googlebook and a phone - I have a whole other set of gripes about the limitations of native Android apps on a $ … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
My first week with the new Android-powered laptops has been about as rocky as anyone’s, but I’ve slowly learned to like them, even if love still feels a ways off. Every moment that’s impressed me has been thanks to Android, whether I’ve been accessing a native version of a useful app or quickly checking my phone notifications from the laptop user interface.

But man, sometimes it just sucks.

Phone connectivity is flaky, app casting is awkward, and file-sharing seems to be flat-out broken. And that’s just the interaction between a Googlebook and a phone — I have a whole other set of gripes about the limitations of native Android apps on a $1,000 laptop.

If Googlebooks ever become a success, Android is going to get the credit. But if it all goes wrong, that’s exactly where the blame will lie too. So far, success feels a lot further away than failure.

Getting started

During setup you can copy every app from your phone, or just a selection.

The Googlebook setup process is Android through-and-through. It’s similarly quick, just a few minutes from beginning to end, including time to register biometric logins, log into a Google account, and connect it to a phone to find your apps and backups. There’s a little variation in the exact setup between the Asus and HP models I’ve been testing, but mostly just whether it defaults to installing every app from your phone or only the desktop-optimized ones.

Things get janky once you’re into the OS, though. Even if you use an Android 17 phone to set up the laptop, it’s unlikely to remain connected afterwards for features like file sharing and app casting. Fully pairing either of my Googlebooks to a phone has required toggling cross-device settings on both devices, multiple restarts, and the occasional prayer, until the two devices find each other. Moving to a new Wi-Fi network broke things for me all over again, requiring a restart of the Googlebook to get the devices back talking to each other — and yes, they need to be on the same Wi-Fi network to talk, and to have Bluetooth enabled too, so the connection won’t work when you’re offline.

My Asus Googlebook has now formed a pretty reliable connection to an Oppo phone I’ve been reviewing, though it still refuses to recognize any other phones; my HP model flits between that Oppo and the Vivo X Fold 6, occasionally connecting to both at once. Yesterday, for the first time all week, it connected to my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, after both laptops had stubbornly ignored that phone for days — even though it’s Google’s own hardware.

Going native

Downloadable episodes! On a laptop! This low key might be my favorite thing about Googlebooks.

I’ve loved elements of the Googlebook experience. It’s great being able to access quick, compact, desktop versions of apps I’d normally be stuck using through a web browser on my MacBook. It’s even better that some of those apps have different functionality for being mobile versions: being able to download series from HBO Max or Netflix and watch them offline means a Googlebook could replace my Android tablet, which is mostly just a device for watching movies on planes at this point.

But many, many more apps are a headache to use on an Android laptop. Some don’t have desktop-optimized versions — the mobile version of Slack is truly unworkable in a desktop environment, and Adobe’s Android apps are pale shadows of their desktop selves. Others claim to be “Optimized for desktop” in the Play Store, but in practice that usually means they’ve stretched the UI to fit a desktop scale and included basic mouse and keyboard support — “basic” being the operative word, with most not recognizing right-clicks or occasionally shifting into a portrait view. “Made for desktop” seems to be the only Play Store tag that really counts for much, and I’ve only seen it on a handful of apps.

Some apps claim to be “Made for desktop,” everything else is likely to feel at least a little awkward.

Even Google’s own apps are often limited. Chrome is the worst offender, since you’re likely to use it so much. Google insists this is a desktop version of the browser, but it lacks feature parity with other platforms: there’s no support for switching profiles, opening tabs in a split view, or creating custom search engine shortcuts. Those are just the omissions I’ve run into from my daily MacBook workflow, and there are no doubt countless more.

And despite Google’s promise that Chromebooks offer the “entire Play Store library,” that isn’t entirely true. I’ve already run into two apps that I simply can’t install from the Play Store — Bluesky and the login authorization tool Okta. It’s not an Intel issue either, as Google alluded to on Monday: the Arm-based HP Googlebook also won’t run either app.

My laptop needs aren’t complex: I spend 90 percent of my time on my work MacBook Air inside Chrome and Slack, and most of the rest in Photoshop or Lightroom. But all four are subpar on a Googlebook right now, and it’s all because they’re fundamentally Android apps that can’t compete with true desktop alternatives.

Casting confusion

If Android apps on your laptop aren’t enough, Googlebooks also let you cast the Android apps on your phone to your laptop.

A dedicated app drawer shows everything installed on your connected phone.

Some version of Android app casting or mirroring has been around before on both Windows and Chromebooks. The difference in Google’s implementation is that instead of mirroring the whole phone UI, you cast specific apps, either through a dedicated app drawer in the taskbar or by tapping into a synced notification from your phone. Those apps still run on the phone itself — which gets a notification that an app is casting — but are controlled via the PC.

It’s not well-suited to streaming music or video, or running multiple apps at once, but that doesn’t seem to be the intent anyway. Where casting shines is in quickly dipping into an app without reaching for your phone and unlocking it, like updating a payment in the settlement app Splitwise or sending a quick message in WhatsApp. I’ve really enjoyed being able to dive in and out of a phone task from my laptop, while minimizing the risk of getting distracted by Instagram.

Casting is clever and mostly works well, but I think I’ve found it useful because I’m new to the Googlebook and haven’t set every app up yet. Google argues it’s designed for apps you might want to use from your laptop but wouldn’t want to install there, but that’s a pretty short list, especially given that installing an Android app is generally quick, painless, and a minimal drain on storage. Long-term, I’m not sure how often I’d want to cast a mobile app when I could just install a native version, especially since you can’t copy and paste between native apps and cast versions, or access the Googlebook file system when casting.

Casting Bluesky from the phone just doesn’t work, made worse because the Bluesky app is unavailable for Googlebooks otherwise.

Even when the cross-device connection runs smoothly, some apps — especially secure ones like my authorization app or banking app — won’t run. Others try to open but don’t work: my credit card app breaks on bootup, while Bluesky renders text illegibly. Casting some apps even create rendering issues when I next open them back on the actual phone.

The rest is a mess too

Then there are the other problems.

Continue On lets you start a task on your phone and pick it up on the Googlebook. It’s great when it works, but that’s rare. Only a handful of apps are supported, and even those trigger inconsistently. It works when I open a Google Drive document, but only sporadically in Gmail, and so far never for Calendar.

Notifications are powerful, but messy, with phone and laptop notifications mixed together. Phone notifications open via app casting, but the system gets confused easily. For various reasons, right now my Slack notifications open a casted phone app rather than the native Googlebook app; WhatsApp notifications don’t come through even from my phone; and I can either get notifications for my work Gmail account or my personal one, but not both at once.

File transfer is entirely broken. While I can see my phone’s storage as a drive inside the file manager, accessing those files is near-impossible. It can take minutes to load up the file system, and minutes more to open or transfer a single 5MB photo. It’s completely unusable. This should be fixable, at least. Quick Share — Android’s equivalent to AirDrop — is also supported, and the same files that take minutes over file transfer share in seconds with Quick Share.

This is what I usually see when I try to open an image from my phone’s file system.

And if I want to copy a file to the laptop, I get to watch this progress bar for a few minutes. 

It’s the Googlebook in a nutshell: the idea is wonderful, the execution entirely lacking. A week in, I’m learning to work around the kinks and headaches of this odd little OS, finding ways to make the most of it and to maximize those moments when my laptop and my phone just work together. When it clicks, it feels like the payoff to a decade and a half of using Android every day.

Right now, that feeling doesn’t hit nearly as often as it needs to, and certainly not enough to make up for the countless times Android just feels broken in this form factor. The question is whether Google — a company with a deserved reputation for giving up when the going gets tough — has the commitment to see this through and turn things around. It’ll need its own teams to fix what’s broken, third-party developers to pledge support en masse, and a rethink of how to integrate native apps with casting from a phone.

When I first saw the Googlebooks a few weeks ago, I really thought one might be my next laptop. After spending a week with them, I’m not so sure. I certainly wouldn’t buy a Googlebook as they are right now, but I wouldn’t rule out an Android laptop in the future — the execution just needs to catch up to the idea.

title: Apple sets Q4 2026 earnings release for November 2
snippet: Apple will announce the results of its fiscal third quarter of 2026 on Monday, November 2. Here’s what to expect. more…
fullText:
Apple will announce the results of its fiscal third quarter of 2026 on Monday, November 2. Here’s what to expect.

Price increases likely to play major role

Apple confirmed today that it will report its Q4 2026 earnings on Monday, November 29.

Following the release of its quarterly results, the company will host a conference call at 2:00 p.m. PT / 5:00 p.m. ET, where John Ternus is expected to participate for the first time as Apple’s new CEO, alongside Apple CFO Kevan Parekh.

For its fiscal Q4 last year, Apple reported $102.47 billion in revenue, up 8%, and $27.47 billion in profit, a whopping 87% increase compared to a $14.7 billion profit in Q4 2024, as a result of a one-time $10.2 billion tax charge related to Apple’s long-running tax dispute in Ireland.

During last quarter’s earnings, Apple said it expected revenue for fiscal Q4 2026 to grow between 9% and 11% year over year, despite an expected 2.5 percentage-point foreign exchange headwind and significantly greater supply constraints affecting the iPhone, Mac, and iPad.

If that pans out, Apple’s revenue should come in between $111.69 billion and $113.74 billion. Apple also guided for a gross margin between 47% and 48%, down from 50.1% last quarter, although that figure included a roughly two-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds.

In practical terms, Apple’s quarterly results will offer the first full-quarter look at the impact of the sweeping price increases it introduced across much of its hardware lineup in late June.

It is also worth noting that, since the reporting period for this fiscal quarter ended in late September, the results are unlikely to provide a meaningful indication of demand for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which also received price increases, as the new models only went on sale on September 18.

That said, Apple’s results will reveal how the company weathered another quarter of memory shortages and rising component costs, clearing the way for Ternus’s first full fiscal quarter as CEO to be reported in late January.

title: Google Cloud announces ‘Gemini agent’ as ‘universal agent for work’
snippet: At Gemini at Work 2026, Google Cloud today announced the “Gemini agent” for enterprise customers. more…
fullText:
At Gemini at Work 2026, Google Cloud today announced the “Gemini agent” for enterprise customers.

Gemini agent is a “new single, universal agent for work” available in the Gemini Enterprise app, Workspace, and third-party services. Google says you can “give it objectives, not instructions.” It can answer questions, handle knowledge work, create media, and write/run code.

“For example, if your manager emails you asking for the latest project update as a slide deck, Workspace Intelligence recognizes that as a delegatable task and gives you a single-click option to pass it to Gemini.”

…you can ask Gemini to set up a meeting with the usual team of regional event leads next week, without supplying a single name or email address. Gemini determines who those people are from the membership of your chat space and the thread from your last event, checks their calendars, and starts an email thread to coordinate a time that works, even with external participants.

Besides functioning as a personal assistant, the Gemini agent can serve as a “team member, where it works on behalf of a group of people, like a project manager within a team, or on behalf of a specific role in an organization, like an analyst in your finance department.”

	

Under-the-hood, the Gemini agent “runs each job on the model that fits best.” This includes both the Gemini and Claude families of models today with support for other private and open models in the future. This is meant to “deliver optimal quality and lower your costs.” It uses sub-agents to “tackle multi-step tasks” and connects with various third-party tools. 

	

Gemini can communicate with these sub-agents to coordinate workflows, including parallel and sequential steps that can run for hours or days.

The agent runs in the cloud for a “single set of memories, context, and one personalization graph.” There are four kinds of memory: 

Session memory: “for the task in front of it, even when it runs for days”

Semantic memory: “a structured knowledge base it builds as it reads documents, talks to people, and works with other agents”

Procedural memory: “for how a job gets done, including skills it writes for itself:

Episodic memory: “everything it has done before”

In Gmail, Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Chat, you can mention @Gemini to invoke. The Gemini agent is available from any device and channel, with command line, Google Workspace, Slack, and Microsoft 365 given as examples. An API allows it to be integrated into third-party applications to surface and operate as a “headless agent, meaning it does not need a dedicated user interface.”

The Gemini agent will see wide availability soon for Workspace customers with select Business and Enterprise plans. It’s currently in private preview.

Typically, Apple’s fall updates for IT are around better way to manage devices, etc. This year, there was an underrated update that I think will be a real win in certain situations: remote AppleCare log collection.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

If you’ve ever opened an AppleCare support case for a hard-to-reproduce issue in your Apple fleet, you know how hard this process is. AppleCare needed a sysdiagnose and getting one meant either physically having the device or walking a user through a series of steps they’ve never done before. That process worked eventually, but it was slow, required the user to be available and willing to help, and, for remote employees or traveling executives, made it appear that IT didn’t have sufficient visibility into the logs of what was happening on the devices. The issue is that they somewhat didn’t.

The harder the issue was to reproduce, the more frustrating this was for IT. By the time you got the logs, the device had rebooted, the macOS state had changed, and you were starting over with your troubleshooting.

TriggerEnhancedLogCollection is your friend

Apple introduced two new device management commands in iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS 27: TriggerEnhancedLogCollection and a cancel command. The process is straightforward. You open an AppleCare case, AppleCare provides you a token, and you pass that token through your device management when you trigger the command. The device collects the logs and uploads them directly to Apple, where they are automatically attached to the ticket with Apple.

The device also reports its status through declarative management at all times, so you can see whether log collection has started, whether it’s finished, whether it’s waiting on user consent, and if the upload is in progress. 

Interactive vs non-interactive

There are two modes for this command, and the difference matters depending on what you’re managing. On iOS, non-interactive mode is available when the device has no passcode and no accounts, so it collects and uploads logs in the background without user involvement. I think this would be applicable in kiosk/POS type settings. On tvOS and Shared iPads, non-interactive is always available.

On macOS, interactive mode is required. The user sees a notification and is prompted to consent to both the log collection and the upload. They can decline, but this is still dramatically better than the old process, but it’s not completely hands-off. The user is in the loop., but at least it’s a simple UI box..

Wrap up

Remote and hybrid work make manual log collection harder and a remote user in a different city experiencing intermittent macOS issues is one of the more challenging support scenarios an IT team can face. With this feature, the moment that Apple’s team asks for logs, you can send the command from your device management console, the device does the work, and Apple has the info it needs to work the case.

title: TrendForce warns of higher notebook prices and weaker demand in 2027
snippet: TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments could decline by a high-single-digit percentage in 2027, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising component costs. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments could decline by a high-single-digit percentage in 2027, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising component costs. Here are the details.

’Brands [to] face difficult trade-offs’

In a report released this week, TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments will decline in 2027, with the drop ranging from low- to high-single digits, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising costs.

TrendForce says the impact will depend on how much of the rising component costs manufacturers pass on to consumers through higher retail prices, rather than absorbing them at the expense of their profit margins.

From the report:

TrendForce’s latest notebook industry research reveals that the primary risk facing the market in 2027 is expected to shift from supply constraints to the impact of rising costs on demand. Global notebook shipments are currently projected to decline by a low-single-digit percentage in 2027.

However, if DRAM and CPU prices remain elevated, brands may be forced to pass more of these costs on to consumers. These higher retail prices could further extend replacement cycles, potentially pushing the full-year shipment decline into the high-single-digit range.

TrendForce says that notebook shipments in 2026 were supported by factors such as improved CPU availability, early purchasing by manufacturers, and replacement demand brought forward from later periods.

With some purchases originally expected in the second half of 2026 and beyond already brought forward, replacement momentum in subsequent periods is likely to weaken. Furthermore, as lower-cost inventories are gradually depleted, brands will face more direct pressure from rising CPU, DRAM, and SSD prices.

The report notes that 68% of the bill of materials for an unnamed “mainstream notebook with a manufacturer’s suggested retail price of US$900” was made up of CPU, DRAM, and SSD costs in the third quarter of 2026.

	

It adds that next year, if component costs keep rising, brands will likely have to choose between raising retail prices and risking weaker demand, absorbing the increases at the expense of gross margins, or reducing specifications, potentially making their products less competitive.

TrendForce says that DRAM supply is “likely to stay tight” next year thanks to AI-related demand, “while PC DRAM faces the risk of limited supply growth.” On the flip side, it expects NAND Flash supply constraints to “ease in the second half of 2027 with new capacity coming online. “

In 2027, brands are therefore unlikely to be able to maintain pricing, specifications, and profitability simultaneously. The extent to which they pass higher costs on to consumers will be a key factor shaping demand.

Finally, the report notes that if tariff pressures don’t increase further, manufacturers could move some notebook production back to China to reduce costs. TrendForce estimates that China’s share of global notebook production will rise from 76% in 2025 to 79% in 2026, potentially exceeding 80% in 2027.

title: iPhone Duo buyers to get a special surprise at U.S. Apple Stores, report says
snippet: According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, iPhone Duo buyers who purchase their device at an Apple Store in the US will be treated to a nice little surprise when they turn it on for the first time. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, iPhone Duo buyers who purchase their device at an Apple Store in the US will be treated to a nice little surprise when they turn it on for the first time. Here are the details.

Cool surprise in store for in-store buyers

When Apple launches the iPhone Duo on October 23, some customers who purchase the device at an Apple Store in the US will be able to have its initial setup screen personalized with their name.

According to Gurman, “Apple retail stores will have a system to customize the boot of the device,” allowing the iPhone Duo to display a greeting containing their name when it turns on for the first time. Gurman says the feature will be exclusive to the iPhone Duo, and support both English and Spanish.

Fun little touch for the iPhone Duo launch: Apple retail stores will have a system to customize the boot of the device with the buyer's name so it says "Hello, Mark" (for example) when it turns on for the first time. (US only, Duo only, English and Spanish).

— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 9, 2026

It is not clear how Apple will implement the feature, or whether it will rely on Presto, the system Apple Stores already use to wirelessly update iPhones without removing them from their boxes.

	

First reported by Gurman in 2023, Presto allows Apple retail employees to turn on an iPhone, install software updates, and turn it off again, all while the device remains sealed in its packaging.

Back to the iPhone Duo, it will be available to pre-order starting Friday, October 16, with deliveries and in-store availability beginning October 23.

Apple recently announced that customers will be able to get ready for iPhone Duo pre-orders beginning October 12, and you can read more about that here.

title: Next-gen Google TV Streamer in the works with microphones, presence sensing, & new remote
snippet: 9to5Google can report that development on a next-generation Google TV Streamer is underway. more…
fullText:
9to5Google can report that development on a next-generation Google TV Streamer is underway. 

According to a source familiar with the matter, the new Google TV device retains the same general design. The width is narrower for a slightly more compact footprint. 

The big upgrade is the presence of microphones on the Google TV Streamer itself. There are cutouts on the slanted, pill-shaped surface that will listen for “Hey Google” commands. 

	

Another new hardware feature is presence sensing. Last year, TCL launched the first Google TV with that capability to turn on the Google Photos screensaver when someone enters the room. If you get close, the display shows ambient information like the time and weather.

	

Meanwhile, the new Google TV Streamer will be powered by a faster processor and offer more storage than the current model’s 32GB.

Google is also updating the included remote. The design is largely the same but with two more shortcuts joining the existing buttons for YouTube and Netflix. Additionally, the Find My Remote button remains on the back of the streaming device. 

We don’t have any information on when this next Google TV Streamer is launching. There was a four-year gap between the Chromecast with Google TV 4K and the Google TV Streamer, with the lower-end HD dongle coming in between the two. This refresh comes as Google raised the price of the existing unit by $50 in August.

title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer is free to play on Amazon Luna
snippet: The long-awaited Star Wars: Galactic Racer launched earlier this week on consoles and PC, and is also free to play on Amazon Luna. more…
fullText:
The long-awaited Star Wars: Galactic Racer launched earlier this week on consoles and PC, and is also free to play on Amazon Luna.

Now this is podracing.

That’s more or less the premise of Galactic Racer. The game takes players to tracks around the galaxy during the New Republic era, including some familiar spaces. Amazon summarizes:

STAR WARS: Galactic Racer is a runs-based, high-stakes reinvention of racing born in the lawless Outer Rim. Set during the era of the New Republic, STAR WARS: Galactic Racer introduces the Galactic League—a high-stakes underground racing circuit where rival racers, dangerous courses, and powerful syndicates collide.

And it’s free on Luna.

	

Amazon’s cloud gaming service has seen quite the reinvention over the past year, and currently includes a rotating library of games you can play for free with an Amazon Prime membership. And that’s where Galactic Racer is available. The game launched on Luna the same day as console and PC in perhaps the most high-profile launch on the service in recent memory, especially seeing as the game retails for $60 on other platforms. 

You can access Luna through the web, but you’ll need an Amazon Prime membership to get the most out of it (including Galactic Racer).

title: Googlebook’s app situation is a mess, and not just because things are missing
snippet: Having been using a Googlebook for the better part of a week, there are any number of headaches I could talk about, but easily the biggest problem I’m running into thus far is the app situation. Frankly, it’s a mess. more…
fullText:
Having been using a Googlebook for the better part of a week, there are any number of headaches I could talk about, but easily the biggest problem I’m running into thus far is the app situation. Frankly, it’s a mess.

Googlebook, like Chromebook, was never going to be in a “good” place for apps. The Android-based platform sets up a more capable foundation for the future but, without a major push from Google and partners, it was always going to result in a rough start. 

And, yeah, it’s a rough start.

The “main” issue is around desktop-class apps and programs. Staples like the Adobe suite are simply not here, and there’s no easy way to replace them. Not to mention the depth of niche apps that have been built out in the Windows and macOS over the decades. At launch, Googlebook was never going to compete with that, though I’d argue that stripping away the Linux support ChromeOS did have isn’t exactly helping matters.

	

The problem I’m finding much more frustrating is around the apps Googlebook can access, and the messy situation around that.

The Google Play Store is your main way to obtain apps on Googlebook. Android apps are the preferred method and, in time, I’m sure that’ll work better than it does today. But, at the moment, Google’s stopgap to varying levels of quality for Android apps on desktop was to give five quality labels to any given app. 

Built for mobile: Hasn’t been tested for desktop

Better on the website: The web app/browser version has full features and/or better performance

Compatible with Desktop: Works with mouse/keyboard controls

Optimized for Desktop: “Adapted for a comfortable desktop experience”

Made for Desktop: “Built for desktop with specialized features and controls”

These are all applied by Google — developers have no direct control.

In my book, that’s wildly confusing for the end user, especially as the Play Store doesn’t link out to where you can use the web app for the Android apps it tries to steer you away from.

And it sadly should steer you away from some apps. 

Telegram is a great example of my frustration. The Android app is “better on the website,” and that’s incredibly true. The Android app is broken on Googlebook in a lot of ways, but the most frustrating is that the enter key doesn’t send a message. But, on the flip side, the web app isn’t that much better, as I’ve frequently run into cases where it misbehaves or even crashes. 

Slack continues to be a daily source of frustration, with the Android app being truly a terrible experience on anything other than a phone, and the web app unable to be installed. This is not some niche or trivial app, it’s something that millions rely on for daily work on their laptops. 

Spotify says that it is “Optimized for desktop” and, while it’s not bad, the phone UI doesn’t even scale as well here as it does on a foldable. It gets better when the “Now Playing” panel is expanded out, but it’s still not on par with other desktop platforms. “Optimized” just feels like the wrong word for this label. “Compatible” feels more apt for this particular example, but Google’s categories are way too specific to let that work.

“Optimized for desktop” according to who, exactly?

	

There’s no easy solution here.

Googlebook is in its early days and, while the foundation presents a better future, the “now” is a huge headache, and one I struggle to get on board with because, well why would you subject yourself to this? Good Windows laptops are easy to find. The MacBook Air is easy to find for $1,099 (cheaper than most Googlebooks!). Good, established platforms that simply don’t have these shortcomings. Why would I give that up for some Android integrations that don’t even work with my phone yet?

Sound off in the comments, I’d love to hear what you think about this problem and how it impacts your view of Googlebook.

title: OLED MacBook Pro to help boost premium display shipments, per report
snippet: A new Counterpoint Research report says Apple’s next-generation MacBook Pro will help drive a 50% increase in OLED notebook display shipments in 2026 alone. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new Counterpoint Research report says Apple’s next-generation MacBook Pro will help drive a 50% increase in OLED notebook display shipments in 2026 alone. Here are the details.

New MacBook Pro and premium AI PCs expected to fuel demand

In a report released today, Counterpoint Research projects that advanced notebook display shipments will grow 11% in 2026 compared to 2025, with OLED notebook display shipments expected to rise 50% for the period.

The report notes that the 11% growth in advanced notebook display shipments will comfortably outperform the broader notebook display market, which Counterpoint says it expects to decline 3% year over year.

Counterpoint says it also expects OLED to widen its lead over MiniLED in the advanced notebook display market, rising from 56% of shipments in 2025 to 75% in 2026, while MiniLED is expected to drop from 44% to 25%.

The research company says part of the growth in OLED notebook panel shipments is expected to come from Apple’s adoption of the technology in its next-generation MacBook Pro, currently rumored to be announced on October 27 with a touchscreen display and a redesigned, significantly lighter chassis.

Here’s Counterpoint:

OLED notebook display shipments are forecast to rise 50% in 2026 and another 24% in 2027. Apple’s anticipated adoption of OLED in next-generation MacBook Pro models, alongside continued demand for premium AI PCs, is expected to drive this growth.

Another factor contributing to OLED’s growth, Counterpoint says, is technology and manufacturing advances such as tandem OLED architectures, which improve brightness, power efficiency, and panel longevity.

Apple already uses tandem OLED in the iPad Pro, where two OLED layers work together to deliver higher full-screen brightness. The company is widely expected to use a similar two-stack tandem OLED architecture for the upcoming 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects OLED notebook panel shipments to grow at a compounded annual rate of 26% between 2024 and 2030, while panel revenue is forecast to grow at 35% per year over the same period.

title: Researchers uncover new DarkSword spyware variant affecting unpatched iPhones
snippet: iVerify released a report today detailing P7 DarkSword, a new variant of the malware associated with the DarkSword iPhone exploit chain uncovered earlier this year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
iVerify released a report today detailing P7 DarkSword, a new variant of the malware associated with the DarkSword iPhone exploit chain uncovered earlier this year. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Earlier this year, Google and iVerify revealed two sophisticated iPhone hacking tools known as Coruna and DarkSword, both of which chained multiple iOS vulnerabilities to compromise devices running outdated system versions.

In DarkSword’s case, once an iPhone was compromised, attackers could deploy additional malware with access to sensitive data.

Coruna targeted devices running iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1, while DarkSword affected iPhones running iOS 18.4 through iOS 18.7.

This led Apple to release system updates for the affected older iOS versions, including iOS 15.8.7, iOS 16.7.15, and iOS 18.7.7. Apple went as far as to take the unusual step of making iOS 18.7.7 available to devices that could install iOS 26, so users who elected not to update to the latest system version would also remain protected against DarkSword.

At the time, Google said DarkSword was being used by multiple commercial surveillance vendors and suspected state-sponsored actors, with attacks observed against targets in Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine.

New DarkSword variant found in the wild

Today, iVerify announced the discovery of P7 DarkSword, a previously unseen variant it found while investigating an infection on the iPhone of an employee at a financial institution just two months ago.

In additional details shared with 9to5Mac, iVerify noted that the P7 expands compatibility to iOS 18.7, up from iOS 18.6 in the earlier variant it had been tracking. Other DarkSword deployments observed by Google had already supported iOS 18.7.

The company also said the threat actor behind P7 is distributing it through malicious ads as part of watering-hole attacks, meaning victims do not necessarily appear to be individually targeted. Instead, users can be caught in broader campaigns simply by encountering malicious or compromised web content.

From the report:

In August 2026 we investigated a DarkSword infection that turned out to be a previously unseen variant, which we call P7 DarkSword. The name P7 comes from the threat actor’s use of the p7_ variable prefix in modifications to original DarkSword’s code. Compared with the variants we usually observe, P7 reduces its on-device footprint, adds on-device keychain and crypto-wallet theft, and adds two way C2 communication with the attacker’s infrastructure. This post describes the investigation, the variant’s capabilities, and the indicators that can be used to detect it._

The report says that P7 DarkSword improves on earlier variants in three main areas: stealth, stability, and functionality. The new variant reduces logging and the number of process injections it performs, uses browser storage to avoid repeatedly exploiting the same device, and expands its data-stealing capabilities.

iVerify also told 9to5Mac that the changes appear to reflect substantial work by the operators rather than simple AI-assisted modifications. The company says P7 is much better at hiding itself and cleaning up its behavior, so previous indicators of compromise (IOCs) are no longer valid.

Most notably, iVerify says P7 can extract Keychain data directly on the iPhone before sending it to the attackers, instead of copying the entire Keychain database for processing elsewhere.

P7 DarkSword can also target crypto-wallet data, and introduces more advanced two-way communication with the attackers’ command-and-control infrastructure.

That two-way communication also gives attackers considerably more control over an infected device. According to iVerify, P7 can receive commands to retrieve arbitrary files, upload photos, inventory installed apps, access Apple Notes databases, collect data from individual app containers, and scan the device’s filesystem.

By default, the spyware checks in with the attackers’ command-and-control server every 15 seconds for new instructions, although that interval can be changed remotely.

It’s worth noting that P7 is not a new iOS vulnerability, but rather a new version of the malware deployed after a successful DarkSword compromise. iVerify does not say which iOS version was running on the device where P7 was discovered in August.

The Free plan also works across Mac, iPhone, iPad, Windows, and Chrome, with the same Snippet library staying in sync across devices.

Granted, the 5-Snippet limit can feel a bit restrictive, particularly since the Free plan only allows one active Snippet to be swapped every two weeks.

title: Google Home update fixes broken smart light color control
snippet: Color LED bulbs were refusing to do their job because of a Google Home bug. Google says the fix is rolling out now. more…
fullText:
Color LED bulbs were refusing to do their job because of a Google Home bug. Google says the fix is rolling out now.

According to a few users on Reddit, Google Home isn’t properly adjusting color on smart bulbs. Users say it hasn’t been limited to just one brand, but devices across multiple brands like Philips Hue, Tuya, and Lumiman. The issue was affecting both voice controls and app controls, which are usually more reliable and easier to adjust. But the color sliders did nothing for affected users.

Google responded to the Reddit thread to say a fix is currently rolling out. The post author has since updated the thread to say their voice commands and app are now reliably controlling bulb color.

The post was barely a day old when Google first let users know it was working on a fix. Just a few hours later, an update was rolling out. The quick turnaround is likely appreciated for this bug because it broke a critical component and selling point for not only Google Home but also smart bulb manufacturers.

	

Color control might have been broken while Google works on other additions to the app. Monthly updates are being released to address the functions and bugs appearing as Google Assistant fades into the background, which has officially happened as of last month.

Were/are you experiencing a bug that broke smart bulb color control? It should be fixed now, but if it isn’t, let us know.

title: Smart ring maker Ultrahuman to roll out biological-age model across UAE
snippet: Ultrahuman and Abu Dhabi will spend the next two years working on research and clinical validation of the model.
fullText:
Ultrahuman, a Bengaluru-based health tech startup best known for its smart rings, has partnered with Abu Dhabi health authorities to develop a biological-age model that it says will eventually be made available to people across the United Arab Emirates.

On Monday, Ultrahuman announced that it had signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Abu Dhabi Public Health Center (ADPHC) to develop and validate the model, which will combine clinical biomarkers with data from wearable devices. The partnership aims to use these signals to estimate how quickly an individual is aging and identify factors — including sleep, activity, cardiovascular health, and metabolism — that may be accelerating or slowing that process.

The partnership marks Ultrahuman’s latest effort to go beyond selling wearable hardware and deploy its health algorithms at a much larger scale. The startup increasingly sees itself as a health-data company, with its smart ring serving as one way to collect information that can underpin algorithms spanning aging, longevity, and other areas of health, CEO Mohit Kumar said in an interview.

“If you look at Ultrahuman as a company, we obviously have the Ultrahuman Ring, which is a way to acquire data from the human body,” Kumar told TechCrunch. “But truly, what we care about is not just the form factor, the ring, but what do we do with this data?”

Working with a government gives Ultrahuman the opportunity to apply its algorithms to a far broader population than its own customer base, Kumar said. The startup has sold around 800,000 smart rings globally so far. The Abu Dhabi partnership is Ultrahuman’s first step toward deploying a health algorithm at a national scale, with the health age model eventually intended to be available to people across the UAE, according to the company.

Even though Ultrahuman is known for its smart rings, Kumar said the biological-age model is being designed to be wearable-agnostic, allowing data from rings, wrist-worn devices, straps, and patches to feed into the system alongside clinical biomarkers. Individuals will eventually be able to access their health age through government digital-health platforms including TAMM and Sahatna, the startup said.

Ultrahuman and ADPHC will spend the next two years working on research and clinical validation of the model. Kumar told TechCrunch that the broader rollout will happen in phases, but did not provide a timeline.

The UAE is already among Ultrahuman’s 10 largest markets and accounts for about 4% to 5% of its overall revenue, Kumar said. The startup has operated in the market for nearly five years and sees about 25% higher retention there compared with its other markets, he noted.

Ultrahuman’s existing customer base gives it a narrower view of the population than a government health system. Its typical users are between 25 and 43 years old, Kumar said, while deploying the model across the UAE would expose it to a much broader range of age groups.

The underlying biological-age model was developed using Ultrahuman’s existing data, combining users’ chronological ages with wearable signals and, for some users, blood-test markers, Kumar told TechCrunch. That allows the startup to track how health markers typically change with age and identify deviations from those patterns.

Kumar stressed the model will not be trained on data from the UAE. “We will deploy an algorithm on the UAE data,” he said, adding that Ultrahuman will not have access to personally identifiable information through the program.

Ultrahuman is not the only smart-ring maker working with Abu Dhabi on preventive health. In May, the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi announced a partnership with Ultrahuman arch-rival Oura to combine the company’s wearable data with the emirate’s longitudinal health data, initially focusing on women’s health and cardiometabolic risk.

Kumar told TechCrunch that Ultrahuman is not aware of another company working with Abu Dhabi authorities on the health age model specifically. While he acknowledged that the government works with multiple health-tech companies, he declined to comment on the scope of Oura’s work with Abu Dhabi.

The parallel partnerships come as Ultrahuman and Oura compete in the smart-ring market while looking to push their businesses beyond wearable hardware and deeper into preventive health. The work with the Abu Dhabi authorities also comes as Ultrahuman is looking to build a smart ring that can run software on the device and even power everything from AI interactions to games.

title: Aaron Sorkin’s ‘The Social Reckoning’ is off to a weak start
snippet: What does this mean for a fall full of movies starring villainous tech CEOs?
fullText:
“The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” is on track to make only $5.5 million at the domestic box office this weekend, according to Sunday estimates.

That’s below the already underwhelming $7 million to $8 million the studio had projected, and it means Sorkin’s new movie is unlikely to become a “Social Network”-sized hit. The earlier film had a $22 million opening weekend and made a total of $97 million domestically (and that’s at 2010 ticket prices). It also won Sorkin an Oscar and became one of most influential on-screen depictions of Silicon Valley and startup culture.

Beyond the fate of a single film, the weekend box office could also offer hints about audience excitement, or lack thereof, as we kick off a fall full of movies starring villainous, real-world tech CEOs. There’s Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” (which also opened this weekend), Nathan Fielder’s apparently uncategorizable Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” (coming next weekend!), and the OpenAI boardroom drama “Artificial” (which has a new distributor after being dropped by Amazon).

Outside of theaters, Netflix also has a series called “The Altruists” coming in November, telling the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of FTX.

As for “The Social Reckoning,” while “The Social Network” was a notable success, the theatrical landscape has changed significantly in the last 16 years. And where the first film focused on the excitement and drama of Facebook’s early days, the sequel is darker and heavier — it’s all about whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision to leak what became known as the Facebook files.

So maybe a movie about Senate hearings and algorithm changes was never going to be a big hit. Or maybe the real audience is among older moviegoers who have only returned sporadically to theaters. And I wonder if critiquing Facebook feels a bit less urgent to audiences who are more likely to be losing sleep over AI.

Maybe just as importantly, the new movie’s reviews just aren’t very good. (For what it’s worth, I enjoyed “The Social Reckoning” but will fully admit that it’s overloaded with Sorkin’s trademark speechifying. And I couldn’t help dreaming about a version directed — like the original — by David Fincher, with a score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.)

 “Musk,” meanwhile, made $69,000 during its opening weekend in four theaters. It will roll out more broadly in the coming weeks, but given its length and subject matter, the documentary will probably reach many more viewers once it starts streaming on HBO Max.

title: MacBook Pro overhaul: entry-level model to gain new design sooner than expected
snippet: Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected.

Normally, when Apple introduces a new MacBook Pro design, it takes a while to trickle down. For instance, the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M1 Pro and M1 Max was introduced in 2021, but the base model MacBook Pro stuck with the 13-inch design until 2023, when it gained the 14-inch chassis with the M3 chip.

Similarly, when Apple redesigned the MacBook Pro in 2016, it wasn’t until 2019 that the entry level model gained the Touch Bar. There’s also a similar story for the 2012 retina MacBook Pro redesign.

This time around though, there’ll only be a roughly 6 month gap before the redesign comes to the entry level.

M7 entry-level with redesign

According to Bloomberg, Apple will be introducing the redesign to the entry level MacBook Pro in early 2027, shortly after debuting it in the high end MacBook Pros, rumored to be called MacBook Ultra. From the report:

Apple is also preparing a revamped entry-level MacBook Pro, code-named K104, for as early as the first half of next year. The 14-inch laptop will adopt a new design in line with what Apple is preparing for higher-end MacBooks with touch screens due between the end of this year and early next year.

It’s worth noting that there’ll also be another entry level MacBook Pro with the current design and the M6 chip, which is currently on track to debut this fall alongside the redesigned high-end MacBook Pros. 

To make things even weirder, those redesigned high-end MacBook Pros are also expected to debut with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, instead of M6 generation chips. Apple recently made a decision to abandon its plans for high end M6 chips to instead accelerate M7.

In short, it’ll look like this:

Fall 2026: Entry-level MacBook Pro with M6/old design, high-end with M5 Pro/Max and new design

Spring 2027: Entry-level MacBook Pro with M7 and new design

Fall 2027: High-end MacBook Pro refresh with M7 Pro/M7 Max

Of course, the redesign is expected to feature a slightly thinner chassis, OLED displays with touch support, and possibly even come with a Dynamic Island.

Wrap up

With the recent price hikes, this is excellent news for some people. I’m sure the redesigned 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro will likely cost over $2500, so if you’re looking to get something more in budget with the M7 chip and the redesign, you’ll only have to wait until the following spring.

	

It’s certainly unfortunate that the $1,999 price point of the entry level MacBook Pro today is what the Pro chip versions cost just under a year ago, but that’s the inevitable reality of this memory shortage.

Are you looking forward to the M7 MacBook Pro with the redesign? Let us know in the comments.
