title: Efferon wants to eradicate the devastating toll of pediatric sepsis
snippet: This Battlefield 200 startup has developed blood-purification tech to save children.
fullText:
Sepsis, an acute inflammation triggered by infection, is a leading cause of childhood mortality, claiming roughly 3 million children under the age of five annually.

Efferon, a startup selected as one of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026’s Startup Battlefield 200, is on a mission to drastically lower that number.

The company has developed a medical device that it says lowers organ failure rates and significantly accelerates recovery in children.

When standard treatments like antibiotics cannot stop the immune system’s overreaction, a patient’s blood must be filtered to remove deadly toxins. That is where Efferon’s devices, of absorbers of dangerous cytokines and toxins, step in to make a critical difference.

Dima Romashin, Efferon’s co-founder and CEO, compares what happens in the body during sepsis to a fire, where an immune response overwhelms the body rapidly. “In a fire, there are two things: the flame itself and smoke that it produces,” he told TechCrunch.

In sepsis, endotoxins are the flames and cytokines are the smoke. Efferon, unlike other devices on the market, has developed a mechanism that can absorb both at once, according to Romashin.

Although Efferon makes absorbers for adults, Efferon NEO, its pediatric device developed specifically for young kids, is proving especially effective. Since children have a significantly lower circulating blood volume, they require medical devices engineered specifically for their physiology, according to Romashin.

In April, Efferon NEO received a CE mark, Europe’s equivalent to FDA approval, making it the first multimodal blood-purification device specifically engineered for pediatric sepsis.

Efferon NEO is used in intensive care units across 30 countries, including European hospitals, Saudi Arabia, and Thailand. The company is now preparing to file for FDA approval and is on track to hit $2 million in annualized revenue by the end of 2026.

The startup’s technology was originally developed by scientists at Moscow State University, including co-founder Ivan Bessonov. Recognizing its potential, Romashin, a serial entrepreneur, stepped in earlier this year as CEO to help commercialize it.

Although Romashin admits that Efferon isn’t growing at the breakneck pace of today’s AI startups, true success for the company is measured by something else entirely: every child who gets to go home.

title: Googlebook improving ‘Better Together’ Android sync features, Samsung support rolling out
snippet: The big selling point for Googlebook is that it’s a desktop platform that deeply integrates with your Android phone but, at launch, those “Better Together” sync features are in a messy place. Google is now rolling out updates, including the bafflingly-missing support for Samsung devices. more…
fullText:
The big selling point for Googlebook is that it’s a desktop platform that deeply integrates with your Android phone but, at launch, those “Better Together” sync features are in a messy place. Google is now rolling out updates, including the bafflingly-missing support for Samsung devices.

There are several core features that work between Android phones and Googlebook including app streaming, notification sync, “Continue On” for compatible apps, and more. But, at launch, not everything works as expected. Some features, like Instant Hotspot, seem to work widely, but others are either inconsistent, slow to activate, or simply unavailable. One of the problems is that it takes a bit of work to fully activate these features.

In a post on Reddit, Google explains that it has started rolling out “smoother first-time setup” for these features, reducing the needed steps to actually set up these cross-device features. A bug where the QR code used to pair your phone continues to show even after Googlebook pairing is complete is apparently also fixed with this update. Google Play Services 26.37 (on the phone) is the version you’re looking for. You can check for Play Services updates through the Play Store. Cross-device Services also needs to be updated to 1.0.1346, again through the Play Store. 

Apparently, these updates also seem to enable support for Samsung devices. 

	

Missing Galaxy smartphone support was perhaps the biggest gap in Googlebook at launch, at least in terms of compatibility. Google originally said this would arrive “in the coming weeks,” a phrase that continues to be incredibly vague.

Here’s Google’s full breakdown of everything you’re looking for:

Confirm your phone runs Android 17: Your Android phone must run Android 17. To check your version, open Settings > About phone > Android version (your phone’s settings may vary). Better Together features work with Pixel and compatible Android 17 phones including Xiaomi, Oppo, OnePlus, Motorola, Lenovo, Honor, Sharp, Sony, Samsung (One UI 9.0), and more.

Check your Bluetooth and Wi-Fi: Confirm your phone and Googlebook use the same personal Google Account with both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on.

Use a private home Wi-Fi network: Hotel, cafe, office, and guest Wi-Fi networks frequently use client isolation, which blocks direct local connections between your phone and laptop. Pause any active VPNs or network DNS blockers and test on a standard home Wi-Fi network.

Update Google Play services: Google Play services must be at version 26.37 or higher. To ensure your phone has the latest version, select Settings > Apps (or Apps & notifications)> See all apps. If Google Play services doesn’t appear, select More and then Show system. Select Google Play services from the app list, then App details (or App details in store). If an update is available, select Update.

Update Cross-device services: Cross-device services must be at version 1.0.1346 or higher. To ensure your phone has the latest version, select Settings, then Apps (or Apps & notifications), then See all apps. Select Cross-device services from the app list, then App details (or App details in store). If an update is available, select Update.

Verify Continue activity sub-toggles: On your phone under Settings, search for Cross-device services > Continue activity, and confirm that Tasks, Apps, Notifications, Files & media sharing are all turned On. 

Restart both your phone and your Googlebook to ensure changes take effect.

Some Samsung Galaxy users have already confirmed that “Better Together” features are working on their Googlebooks following these updates.

Missing Samsung support was initially attributed to missing updates on Samsung’s end by some, but it sounds like everything is worked out at this point. You’ll still need One UI 9, though, which is only rolled out to a small portion of Samsung’s device catalog at this point.

Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17

Sound off in the comments below if you’ve been able to use any of these new Googlebook features, or if you even bought a Googlebook in the first place.

title: Formula 1 on Apple TV is getting Dolby Atmos, starting this month
snippet: Beginning with the U.S. Grand Prix weekend on Friday, October 23, Apple TV will offer Formula 1 coverage in Dolby Atmos on supported devices. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Beginning with the U.S. Grand Prix weekend on Friday, October 23, Apple TV will offer Formula 1 coverage in Dolby Atmos on supported devices. Here are the details.

’Bringing exceptional picture and sound together to capture the full intensity of the sport’

Apple and Dolby Laboratories announced a new partnership to bring Dolby Atmos to Apple TV’s live Formula 1 coverage, starting with the U.S. Grand Prix weekend, which begins October 23 in Austin, Texas.

Apple says Dolby Atmos will join “Dolby Vision to deliver an even more immersive viewing experience,” putting “fans at the heart of the action, surrounding them with the energy, drama, and emotion of Formula 1.”

From team radio communications and race commentary to the roar of the engines, on-track battles, and the intensity of the pit lane, Dolby Atmos brings the unmistakable sounds that define the sport to life.

Here’s Oliver Schusser, Vice President of Apple Music and International Content at Apple, on the announcement:

“We’re always looking for new ways to make Formula 1 on Apple TV even better for fans. […] The sound of Formula 1 is such an important part of what makes the sport so exciting, and with Dolby Atmos joining Dolby Vision, fans can experience the energy and intensity of every Grand Prix in a whole new way. It’s another example of how we’re continuing to innovate across the viewing experience to bring fans closer to the action.”

It’s worth noting that Apple TV’s streaming rights for Formula 1 still include only the U.S., but don’t require an extra subscription on top of the Apple TV subscription.

Apple recently made the Bahrain Grand Prix available to stream for free in the U.S., and has also partnered with Netflix to bring Formula 1: Drive to Survive Season 8 to Apple TV in the U.S. As part of the same collaboration, the 2026 Canadian Grand Prix was streamed live on both Apple TV and Netflix in the U.S.

Apple secured the U.S. streaming rights to Formula 1 in 2025 as part of a five-year deal beginning with the 2026 season, and has previously indicated it wants to expand its F1 coverage into additional markets.

Apple’s broader relationship with Formula 1 also includes “F1: The Movie,” which won the Academy Award for Best Sound earlier this year and remains Apple’s biggest theatrical success to date.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

title: Google starts rolling out its upgraded Pixel screen savers to the Pixel 9
snippet: When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets. more…
fullText:
When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets.

A select group of users are starting to spot these screensavers being added to older Pixels, beginning with the Pixel 9, as reported by Android Authority. Earlier Pixels did have support for a basic screensaver tool, but with this upgrade, every option available on Google’s latest releases have finally been backported to its 2024 hardware. The update appears to include a pop-up demo of these new options, along with everything currently available as of the Pixel 11’s launch. Clock, Charge, Weather, Photos, and Home Controls are all available, and can be swiped through at will. And speaking of Charge, it too seems to be headed to the Pixel 10 series, after having been exclusive to the Pixel 11 for the past two months.

Unfortunately, it does seem like this is one of Google’s classic slow rollouts. There aren’t a massive amount of reports from Pixel 9 users that these styles are live on their devices, implying it might take a few weeks before reaching everyone. The same goes for Charge on the Pixel 10, with plenty of Redditors confirming they have yet to see that specific style arrive.

More on Pixel:

title: XREAL Aura with Android XR start at $1,279
snippet: XREAL’s first pair of Android XR glasses, XREAL Aura, finally have a price tag – $1,279. more…
fullText:
XREAL’s first pair of Android XR glasses, XREAL Aura, finally have a price tag – $1,279.

XREAL makes glasses that aren’t a traditional VR headset, nor are they the smart glasses we’ve imagined for the future. They sit somewhere in between, with a display that sits atop a see-through lens so you can mix the display’s content with the real world around you, no cameras needed. 

As we noted in a review of XREAL One Pro, though, the base experience of using the glasses to display content from a USB-C device like a laptop, phone, or handheld game console is a bit limited. Android XR’s promises are set to deliver a big upgrade to the experience, and that’s exactly what XREAL has been building.

XREAL Aura is effectively the same core idea, just with an included puck that has a battery, processing power, and Android XR. And it starts at $1,279, the company has today confirmed. The price of XREAL Aura was the missing puzzle piece for months, and it’s actually well below the company’s promise of “under $1,500.”

	

That’s for the base 12GB/256GB model, with an upgraded version costing a bit more:

XREAL Aura 12GB/256GB: $1,279

XREAL Aura 16GB/512GB: $1,499

There’s no charge for the medium or large size difference.

As far as actually putting in an order, XREAL says the initial delivery wave will arrive “before the holidays,” with a second wave presumably arriving sometime in early 2027. You have to purchase a $199 “Priority Deposit” to place a pre-order, with the cost going towards the price of your Aura glasses.

Pre-orders open later this month.

title: The Feds Might Do Something About Those Distractingly Bright Headlights
snippet: NHTSA blames current vehicle standards for making it hard for carmakers to use the latest headlight tech.
fullText:
The blinding glare of LED headlights from oncoming traffic searing your retinas may become a thing of the past. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced this week that it intends to update vehicle lighting standards as part of changes to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 108. 

In simple terms, it means the administration could move to make LED headlights less blinding. The last time lighting standards were updated was 25 years ago, which is one reason US lighting regulations have allowed vehicles to have skull-searing headlights not typically seen in Europe or Japan.

“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in a press statement. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.” 

			

More from CNET

LED headlights make sense for an electric car, as they put minimal power drain on the batteries.

James Martin/CNET

The new regulations will update rules for LEDs, dusk sensors, automatic high beams and replaceable light sources. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will appoint up to 18 industry stakeholders, safety advocates and technical experts to evaluate how headlamp height and aim affect driver visibility as part of efforts to align US vehicles with international safety standards.

Since 2022, companies have been allowed to use adaptive driving beams, which are dynamic systems that can keep high beams on while dimming portions of the beam to avoid glare to oncoming drivers. However, the implementation of this policy doesn’t match the same standards seen in Europe.

Some companies are already positioned to take advantage of the changes with their upcoming models. Rivian, with its R1T and R1S Gen 2 models, already uses this type of lighting. Audi will debut its 2027 Q9 flagship SUV with the technology.

Better headlights would come as a welcome change for many drivers. Gripes about blinding LED headlights are well documented, with an entire subreddit of 12,000 members dedicated to the topic. Reuters, citing a study from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, says that from 2015 to 2023, headlight glare was cited as a factor in one or two out of every 1,000 nighttime crashes across 11 US states, though it noted that this is far fewer than the number of crashes caused by insufficient visibility.

Anecdotally, complaints about the brightness of headlights are a common topic in one of my group chats, with one member saying they often feel like the headlights are radioactive and can “X-ray and skeletonize oncoming drivers.” 

NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Gas Stoves Create Indoor Air Pollution Risk in Commercial Kitchens, Study Finds
snippet: The study also makes a case for gaps in kitchen worker protection.
fullText:
Following a July study that found switching from a household gas stove to an electric one can improve asthma symptoms, a new peer-reviewed study published on Tuesday concluded that workers in restaurant kitchens using gas and propane appliances are exposed to air pollution and heat levels that exceed health guidelines.

The National Restaurant Association reports that over 15.7 million Americans work in the food service industry. According to a statement, about five million of them spend all their working hours in the kitchen.

Published in the scientific journal Environmental Research Letters and in collaboration with chef Christopher Galarza, the study was conducted by researchers from the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, the New York University Grossman School of Medicine and PSE Healthy Energy, an independent scientific research institute specializing in bringing science to energy policy. 

			

More from CNET

According to the statement, this is the first US study to compare air quality and heat levels in restaurant kitchens that use gas appliances with those that use all-electric appliances under real-world working conditions. The study is part of PSE Healthy Energy’s Methane and Health Initiative, which uncovers air quality and health risks associated with methane sources to protect public health and the climate. 

Researchers measured air temperature and air pollutants produced by gas stoves: methane, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and benzene. Measurements were taken in five employee work areas, both during service and overnight, in 21 gas kitchens, three propane kitchens and three all-electric kitchens in California, New York and Pennsylvania. 

“Everyone likely has a favorite restaurant or fast food chain, but most people probably haven’t thought about the equipment being used and how that affects what the staff is experiencing in the kitchen area,” Drew Michanowicz, principal scientist at PSE Healthy Energy, told CNET in an email.

Air pollution findings

When kitchens are not properly ventilated, pollutants can build up and cause harmful health effects, though this depends on individual sensitivity and exposure level. 

During the study, it was discovered that in most of the gas and propane kitchens included, at least one health guideline for pollutant exposure was exceeded during cooking hours. 

About 70% of gas kitchens in the study surpassed the US Environmental Protection Agency’s 1-hour outdoor air standard for nitrogen dioxide. The outdoor standard was used because there is no comparable indoor standard in the US. 

In kitchens with gas or propane appliances, about 170 cumulative hours (about four full work weeks) were recorded in which nitrogen dioxide concentrations exceeded the World Health Organization’s hour-averaged exposure recommendation. This recommendation is roughly equal to the EPA’s outdoor standard, and both apply to the general population.

One kitchen’s 15-minute average nitrogen dioxide level exceeded the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health’s recommended short-term workplace exposure limit.

Nitrogen dioxide can cause reduced lung function, increased asthma attacks, increased airway inflammation, and worsened cough and wheezing. This gaseous air pollutant has even been tied to causing asthma in children. 

The study also found that carbon monoxide and benzene concentrations exceeded California’s 1-hour exposure guidelines in three and five gas kitchens, respectively. Carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms can range from a headache and dizziness to passing out and death. Benzene, on the other hand, is a carcinogen that has been linked to a higher risk of leukemia and other blood cell cancers.

By comparison, no all-electric kitchen exceeded pollution-exposure health guidelines during cooking hours. 

“This study emphasizes that the concentrations of pollutants in commercial kitchens with gas-fired appliances can reach levels even higher than what we’ve previously observed in homes with gas stoves,” Yannai Kashtan, an air quality scientist at PSE Healthy Energy, told CNET in an email.

Those actually working in the kitchen aren’t the only ones who could be affected.Rhenizara S/Getty Images

Overnight levels matter too

Even outside cooking hours, exposure remains a concern, according to new evidence from the study. 

When gas appliance pilot lights remain lit, and ventilation is turned off, cleaning crews and staff arriving early risk exposure to pollutants. About 71% of the gas kitchens with overnight monitoring recorded higher levels of nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane and benzene overnight than during service hours.

Aside from contributing to climate change, high concentrations of methane can displace oxygen in the air, causing fatigue, rapid breathing, vomiting, collapse, convulsions, organ damage and death. 

When you consider that commercial gas appliances are also used in hospitals, schools and other buildings, the health concerns extend beyond restaurant kitchens.  

None of the all-electric kitchens exceeded pollutant guidelines overnight. 

Temperature findings

When it came to heat health guidelines, about 68% of gas kitchens with temperature data exceeded 90 degrees Fahrenheit, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s proposed high-heat threshold.

Even when temperatures outside were below 75 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 of 13 gas kitchens exceeded 90 degrees Fahrenheit, meaning that high heat in commercial kitchens isn’t directly tied to the weather. 

When a temperature monitor was attached to a chef’s shoulder during a 5-hour cooking session, the average temperature was 92 degrees Fahrenheit, with a maximum of 106 degrees Fahrenheit.

Guidelines differ between the general population and the workplace, which could put workers’ health at risk.andresr/Getty Images

A guideline gap in kitchen worker protection

The study compared its findings with both EPA and WHO guidelines for the general population, which prioritize health protection, and with NIOSH and OSHA guidelines, which are occupational. Researchers found fewer instances of kitchens exceeding workplace thresholds. 

“Compared to benchmarks for the general population, occupational thresholds are higher because they serve a different purpose by also accounting for industry cost and technical feasibility,” Kashtan said. “If work environments are exceeding health-based thresholds but are compliant with the occupational limits that govern enforcement, this points to a gap in health protection for commercial kitchen workers.”

The study’s limitations

Due to the scarcity of all-electric commercial kitchens, only three were used in this study. However, the researchers stated in the study that their findings remain consistent with prior research on nitrogen dioxide concentrations from gas versus electric appliances. 

As about 80% of end-use energy in US commercial cooking is gas, the small number of all-electric kitchens used in the study also reflects the current restaurant industry. 

Only restaurant kitchens in three states were used, so this may not reflect the broader US. Participation was voluntary and partly facilitated through professional partnerships, so selection bias may have been introduced, especially given that kitchens willing to participate likely had better working conditions. 

While sampling locations were chosen to account for different worker roles in the kitchen, pollutant measurements may differ from actual exposure due to a worker’s movement, health, posture and proximity to emission sources. These locations also weren’t monitored continuously; instead, they were sampled for 5 to 12 minutes per cycle. 

Particulate matter and WBGT, which measures occupational heat stress, were not measured. 

Ensure that your range hood is maintained and turned on when cooking.SBenitez/Getty Images

Restaurant recommendations

Based on this study, Michanowicz has three recommendations for worker protections in commercial kitchens that use gas appliances. 

First, it’s important to ensure that ventilation systems are properly maintained, as these are usually the first line of defense against pollution and excess heat. However, even with these systems in place, restaurant workers who work directly over a cooking surface can still be exposed to pollution and heat before they reach the ventilation system. 

While converting a commercial kitchen from gas to electric can be challenging and costly, focusing on electrifying gas ranges and fryers first can yield the greatest benefits for indoor air quality. 

“There are also additional benefits that chefs we worked with have mentioned, such as higher worker productivity due to more comfortable kitchen temperatures, reduced cleaning times and reduced burn and explosion risks,” Michanowicz said.

Lastly, for workers in commercial kitchens during off-hours, including cleaning crews, when pilot lights are still on, ventilation systems should be turned on. This applies to workers who arrive early in the morning, as pollution will have built up overnight. 

Gas stove household advice

The recommendations for those with gas stoves at home aren’t dissimilar. 

“The best way to reduce gas combustion pollution is to eliminate the source – the gas flame – and to get an electric radiant or induction stove,” said Kashtan. 

However, if that’s not possible due to cost or because one is a renter, cooking can still be partially electrified with air fryers, electric kettles, rice cookers and portable induction hobs. 

And when you do use your gas stove, always make sure your range hood is on, and consider putting an air purifier in your kitchen.

Over the past 12 years, Anna has also written for the LA Times, Elle, Bust Magazine, Dazed, Apartment Therapy, Well+Good and more. title: Googlebooks can’t install the Slack web app on day one
snippet: Googlebook is now on sale and shipping to customers and, on day one at least, they can’t install the Slack web app. more…
fullText:
Googlebook is now on sale and shipping to customers and, on day one at least, they can’t install the Slack web app. 

Googlebook as a platform relies on two main forms of apps. The first is native Android apps, as Googlebook OS is, at its core, Android. That’s what you’ll use for many experiences including Gemini, Google Photos, music apps, and more. Others, like Gmail and YouTube, instead rely on progressive web apps. That term might sound familiar if you’re a long-time Chromebook user, as Chromebooks bet pretty heavily on progressive web apps (PWAs).

That history aside, Googlebooks directly tell their users to use Slack through the web app. The Play Store puts up a banner saying that Slack is “better on the website” when you try to download the Android app. 

That’s correct, frankly, as Slack’s Android app has terrible support for anything besides a standard smartphone. 

	

But the Slack web app cannot be installed on a Googlebook at this time.

	

Trying to install the Slack web app as a PWA on Googlebook results in an error message saying that “this app cannot be installed.” You can still create a shortcut that opens as a Chrome tab, but it won’t open in a window. 

Other PWAs we’ve tested including Photopea, Squoosh, SnapDrop, and others seem to be working fine. It’s unclear why Slack in particular is broken, but it’s hard to imagine it’s the only PWA not working on Googlebook on day one. More importantly, Slack is a mainstay in the modern workspace, so lacking any form of desktop-level Slack support on day one is sure to leave a poor impression on early Googlebook adopters.

Update: Google, in a statement, says that Slack is not a “compliant” PWA but that Googlebook will add support for manual installation soon.

Installing PWAs is fully supported on Googlebooks. But, the Slack web app isn’t a compliant PWA. Chrome on ChromeOS allows manual installation even though it’s not a PWA. This capability will also be coming to Chrome on Googlebooks soon.

title: Google Wallet rolling out stacked card list redesign on Android
snippet: After updating the bottom half of the homepage earlier this year, Google Wallet for Android is rolling out a stacked list redesign for accessing credit and debit cards. more…
fullText:
After updating the bottom half of the homepage earlier this year, Google Wallet for Android is rolling out a stacked list redesign for accessing credit and debit cards.

The previous design made use of a carousel to show your stored payment methods. This design showed just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google allowed you to reorder cards and set a default one.

	

With this stacked redesign, the homepage shows one full card preview and the sliver of a second at the top. To expand, you tap or swipe down to enter the fullscreen layout that shows most of each card. “Manage payment methods” at the bottom lets you arrange the order and set the default.

You select a card to tap-to-pay. To see card details and transaction history, there’s a new settings gear icon in the top-right corner. This adds an extra step compared to the previous approach.

	

This approach is nice for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom. There are no other changes to the Google Wallet homepage.

This redesign started appearing in September and is now seeing broader availability. It’s rolling out via a server-side update and appeared on several devices we checked today.

title: The founder’s guide to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Everything you need to know
snippet: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is built around one question: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era? Our programming and speaker lineup reflect that.
fullText:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is built around one question: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era? Our programming and speaker lineup reflect that, based on the feedback we’ve gotten from the community and the reality on the ground. And everything kicks off in just a few days, act now before your chance to save $100 on your pass comes to an end.

Last year at Disrupt, we spoke with founders about their experiences and discovered the results of their attendance firsthand. One founder saw a 3x oversubscription rate after their confirmation for Startup Battlefield and more than 100 investor inbounds helping fuel conversations about a future fundraising round. Another founder had nearly 30 back-to-back conversations with investors who flocked to them after a pitch onstage and followed them to their booth.

That’s not the exception at Disrupt — that’s the point. And those opportunities aren’t just available for Battlefield finalists. Every conversation in the Expo Hall or in a Side Event can create an opportunity for your startup. For years, whether it’s been held in New York, San Francisco, or elsewhere, Disrupt has brought together thousands of founders, investors, startup team members, and tech leaders.  

We’re keeping that mission alive at SF’s Moscone West, this October 13-15 with a packed lineup of speakers, more than 200 expert sessions, a wealth of organized and serendipitous networking opportunities, and most of all, the chance to be in the same room as the person who could change your nascent idea for a company or your current startup’s trajectory.

This guide is for the founders out there who are just learning about Disrupt, who need a refresher, or are skeptical of whether it’s worth it. TechCrunch has been around for more than 20 years; we can take it. And before you dive in, we have two discounts that run up until Disrupt begins you should be know about. Founders can bring a team member along for 50% off their ticket by following this link, or you can help laid off members of your network find their next opportunity at Disrupt with our steep discount of Expo+ passes.

Image Credits:TechCrunch / Slava Blazer Photography

The reality of what makes Disrupt, Disrupt 

If you’re asking Claude or ChatGPT if TechCrunch Disrupt is worth it, you’re not alone. The reality is that Disrupt is a unique event, and it’s happening at a unique time for the startup community.

This year’s Disrupt isn’t about predicting the future of AI; it’s about building companies in it. Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology.  

Whether you’re raising your first round, scaling your team, or deciding how AI changes your product, every session is designed to answer one question: “What can I take back to my company on Monday morning?”

The founders Disrupt empowers 

Disrupt works a bit differently, depending on where you are in your founding journey, with different tracks you can follow to make the most of the three days:

Pre-seed and idea stages 

You’re here to pressure-test your thesis, meet your first angel or pre-seed investors, and figure out who else is building in your space. Prioritize the Builders Stage, the Startup Battlefield semifinalist pitches, and the Expo Hall, along with roundtables tied to your industry and conversations you’ll want to learn more from.

Early revenue or actively raising 

You’re here for capital and validation above all else, and your time is valuable. Prioritize our investor-matchmaking tools and the connections that come with your Founder Pass, including the networking tools in our app. You also get access to the Deal Flow Café, where we foster one-on-one conversations between founders and investors.  

And when your schedule isn’t packed with dealmaking, learn from VC perspectives and fundraising-focused sessions at the Builders Stage.

Scaling, hiring, in search of partnerships 

You’re here in search of talent, strategic partners, and market visibility. Those same networking tools and opportunities can help you meet potential hires and partners and deepen those connections or make new ones. Disrupt’s Side Events aren’t to be missed — there’s one for every industry, interest, or post-event vibe you could be looking to find.

Startup Battlefield: The most iconic pitch competition 

The Startup Battlefield winner’s reveal packs the Disrupt stage and is each year’s capstone event. But it’s the lead-up to that $100,000 check and the deluge of attention the winner receives that’s the most valuable for founders attending Disrupt.

The 200 startups chosen on August 20 to compete go through a rigorous prep process and get the opportunity to pitch onstage in front of top-tier VCs and the Disrupt crowds. You’ll also get to watch those pitches, take notes, learn from the peaks and valleys, and potentially meet the teams behind the ideas and innovations. It could be in a follow-up meeting or just walking through the halls of Moscone.  

And if that all leaves you inspired, here’s an insider tip: Most Battlefield participants, and several winners, have gone through the process multiple times. We’re no longer taking applications for 2026’s competition, but we’re expanding the program to more international markets, and the 2027 process will be similar to this year’s, so take note for the future!

The founder-focused programming 

Disrupt 2026 spans several stages, each built around a different founder need:

Disrupt Stage: The biggest conversations in technology, featuring the founders, CEOs, and industry leaders defining what’s next. These are the conversations you’ll be talking about long after Disrupt ends.

Builders Stage: The tactical playbook for building a startup. From fundraising and hiring to GTM, product, and scaling, every session is designed to give founders practical advice they can put to work immediately.

AI Stage: AI isn’t the future — it’s the present. Learn how the fastest-growing startups are building, deploying, and monetizing AI, with practical lessons on agents, models, infrastructure, and what it takes to win in the AI era.

Real World AI Stage: AI is moving beyond the screen and into the physical world. Explore how robotics, autonomous systems, manufacturing, healthcare, and defense are turning AI breakthroughs into real-world products and businesses.

Smart Money Stage: Follow the money. From fintech and stablecoins to payments, embedded finance, and AI-driven financial services, this stage explores how technology is reshaping the movement of capital.

Smart Systems Stage: Every AI breakthrough depends on the infrastructure behind it. Discover the innovations in chips, compute, energy, networking, and data centers that will determine the next generation of technology companies.

Image Credits:TechCrunch / Slava Blazer Photography

Conversations you can only get at Disrupt 

RJ Scaringe (Rivian): Building a generational company. 

Panos Panay (Amazon): Designing products people love. 

Paolo Ardoino (Tether): Money, AI, and infrastructure. 

Toni Schneider and Rose Wang (Bluesky): Can social start over? 

Amjad Masad (Replit): Every founder becomes technical. 

Andrew Feldman (Cerebras): Winning the AI compute race. 

And that’s just the beginning — we’ll have more speakers to announce as we get closer to Disrupt. Check out the full lineup of speakers across all stages and events here.

How to get the most bang for your buck at Disrupt 

Disrupt’s prices increase as we get closer to the event, but we have a couple of promotions for Founders looking to save. You can save 50% on a second ticket by following the link here, and bring a coworker or co-founder along for the ride.  

If there are colleagues in your network who have been impacted by layoffs who you’d like to have join up, we have an option for them as well, with a special $75 Expo+ Pass available at a limited volume for those impacted by cutbacks this year.

Your time at Disrupt is valuable, too, so before you head there, check on our regularly updated schedule of speakers and Side Events, get ahead of competitors’ schedules by booking your networking opportunities in advance, and get your own elevator pitches in order to make the most of those magical Disrupt moments that can come at any point October 13-15!

title: Google officially teases Fitbit Edge tracker, confirms October 12 launch
snippet: Google has dropped an official teaser for its Fitbit Edge tracker and confirmed an October 12 launch, just a few days away. more…
fullText:
Google has dropped an official teaser for its Fitbit Edge tracker and confirmed an October 12 launch, just a few days away.

In a brief post on social media (Twitter/X, Instagram) Google simply says:

Get an Edge on your health. 10.12.2026.

It’s simple and to the point, and says a lot while not saying much at all. The teaser confirms the “Edge” branding of the new tracker, which is said to follow the Air in Fitbit hardware lineup. The Fitbit Edge is then confirmed to launch on October 12, this coming Monday.

	

Google’s teaser image just barely hints at the display we’ve seen in leaks, while also confirming that the company’s “Canyon” color scheme will continue through from the Pixel Watch 5. It’s also obvious that the Edge has a metal chassis.

	

Leaked Fitbit Edge renders

Other leaks have detailed 7-day battery life, Gemini integration, iPhone support, and more for the upcoming Fitbit Edge. Pricing is expected to be around $180 — not too far above the screen-less Fitbit Air, but well below the Pixel Watch 5’s $400 entry price.

title: ‘HomePad’ is coming next week, with three features I’ve long wanted
snippet: Apple’s long-rumored ‘HomePad’ product is finally set to be unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are three HomePad features I’ve been waiting a long time for. more…
fullText:
Apple’s long-rumored ‘HomePad’ product is finally set to be unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are three HomePad features I’ve been waiting a long time for.

#1: Apple Photos on a digital picture frame

Digital picture frames are nothing new. But I’ve never owned one, in large part for two reasons:

All my pictures live in Apple Photos

I don’t want to manually add pictures to the digital frame

There are currently zero digital picture frames with native Apple Photos integration for an effort-free experience. But with the HomePad, rumors indicate there’s a Photos face available that will automatically cycle through pictures from Apple Photos.

This is exactly what I’ve been wanting for years. I hope to put several HomePads throughout the house so they can surprise and delight me with memories at every turn (while providing other key features too).

#2: Apple Music in the home with lyrics onscreen

I own a few HomePods, and enjoy listening to music with them. But what I’ve really wanted for a long time is the chance to see lyrics while listening.

Thanks to AirPlay, I can do this with my iPhone while music plays through the HomePod. I rarely do this, though, because I try to avoid pulling my phone out as much as possible with family around.

With HomePad though, all signs point to the Music app letting you view lyrics onscreen while a song is playing. I’m terrible at picking up lyrics just by ear, so I’m excited for the chance to better learn songs while staying in the moment with family members when we’re listening together.

#3: Siri AI in a HomePod-like device with a display

	

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri. Unlike the old Siri on my HomePods, Siri AI can handle basically any question you throw at it. And with the HomePad, not only will Siri’s intelligence get a boost—it will also be able to show visuals in its responses.

I ask Siri on my HomePods to do basic things like set reminders, or provide info on the weather. But with Siri AI on the HomePad, I imagine I’ll turn to Siri far more often than I ever have. That’s already been true with Siri AI on my iPhone.

Having Apple’s new AI assistant all throughout the house, and equipped with a display for showing visual results, should prove a big improvement from my current HomePod setup.

Are you interested in Apple’s HomePad, and if so, what do you imagine using it for? Let us know in the comments.

title: Samsung rolling out Android 17 for more Galaxy devices in the US
snippet: Samsung’s Android 17 rollout is speeding up, with more last-gen Galaxy devices now getting One UI 9 updates in the US. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s Android 17 rollout is speeding up, with more last-gen Galaxy devices now getting One UI 9 updates in the US.

After a delay, Samsung started rolling out its Android 17 update more broadly to Galaxy devices at the end of September. It started off with the Galaxy S26 series, but the update is now rolling out a bit more broadly in the US market.

That includes the Galaxy Z Fold 7 and Galaxy Z Flip 7, which are now getting Android 17 in the US. SamMobile notes that Fold 7 owners on T-Mobile and Verizon are both seeing the update land, while it’s showing up for Galaxy Z Flip 7 owners on AT&T. Unlocked units are likely to see the update arrive in the next few days or so.

Meanwhile, Galaxy S25 is also seeing its stable update in the States, apparently also only on certain carrier-locked variants. SammyGuru points out Verizon support, with the update also showing up for Galaxy S25 FE and Galaxy S25 Edge alongside the core lineup.

	

If you have Fold 7, Flip 7, or any Galaxy S25 device, head to Settings > Software update > Download and install to see if the update is available!

title: iFixit tears down Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, finds mixed repairability results
snippet: Concluding iFixit’s teardown sequence for Apple’s September launches, iFixit today published the teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s what they found. more…
fullText:
Concluding iFixit’s teardown sequence for Apple’s September launches, iFixit today published the teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s what they found.

iFixit tears down Apple Watch Ultra 4

After applying heat to the new Apple Watch Ultra 4’s screen, iFixit’s Shahram Mokhtari uses the company’s new metal pick to pry the screen open, exposing the battery and the Taptic Engine.

He notes that replacing the 2.444 Wh battery (versus 2.313 Wh in the Ultra 3) still requires removing the screen, which remains a significant repairability drawback. The four screws on the bottom of the case provide access only to the sensor assembly on the underside of the back cover and the S11 chip on the case itself.

Once the screen is unglued, though, removing the battery and disconnecting the display’s press connector seems straightforward enough, provided that the initial step was done carefully enough to avoid slicing through any of the flex cables underneath.

That said, with no significant improvements in repairability, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 scored 4/10 on iFixit’s repairability scale, the same as its predecessor.

iFixit tears down Apple Watch Series 12

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 revealed a slight repairability improvement, with Apple adding stretch-release adhesive and a pull tab that make the 1.461 Wh battery (versus 1.403 Wh in the 46mm Series 11) easier to remove.

Still, as with the Apple Watch Ultra 4, the Series 12 also requires prying off the glued display to get inside, which remains the biggest obstacle to repairs. Mokhtari noted that the tolerances around the Series 12’s display are even tighter than on the Ultra 4, requiring enough force to make him concerned about potentially damaging the screen.

Mokhtari also noted that Apple replaced the ZIF connector and tape used for the display on previous models with a simpler press connector.

The tradeoff is that replacing the screen now also requires removing and replacing the battery, “which, if you’ve come this far, why wouldn’t you?” he adds.

All in all, the modest repairability improvements were enough for iFixit to give the Series 12 a 4/10 repairability score, a 1-point bump from the last base-model Apple Watch it scored.

For comparison, iFixit gave Google’s Pixel Watch 5 a 9/10 repairability score, noting that its display can be removed with just two Torx screws and a gasket, while its battery can also be removed without dealing with adhesive.

title: Googlebook’s hidden ‘Glowbar Disco’ turns your laptop’s lid into a light show — how to find it
snippet: Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank. more…
fullText:
Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank.

The Glowbar on Googlebook is a carryover from the iconic light bar on the original Chromebook Pixel. It doesn’t function quite the same, lacking the fun and useful “knock knock” gesture that Google’s original offered, but it still shows battery on plug-in, and serves as a nice accent too.

But, hidden behind the scenes is more control over the glowbar.

The “Glowbar Disco” app is an Easter egg buried deep within the OS, and even Google’s Alexander Kuscher admits it might be “too hard to find.” The app itself lets you set the Glowbar on a Googlebook to show a constant color, a preset animation, a gradient of colors, or even sync with music. It leaves the Glowbar active whenever the machine is turned on and the Disco app is open, and it’s a super fun little addition.

	

Finding the app, though, is not exactly an easy task. 

You’ll have to go to Settings > Apps then allow the search function to show system apps, then search for “Glowbar Disco.” From there you can launch the app, but you’ll need to repeat that process every time you want to access it. And, if you close the app, the effects stop.

If you ask me, this should be baked into the Settings because it is very fun. Hopefully that’ll change in time — Googlebooks certainly need a lot of updates.

snippet: Apple could showcase its new co-developed smart home accessories as soon as next week. Ahead of that, a new leak today reveals a HomeKit feature exclusive to these “second-party” accessories. more…
fullText:
Apple could showcase its new co-developed smart home accessories as soon as next week. Ahead of that, a new leak today reveals a HomeKit feature exclusive to these “second-party” accessories. 

An exclusive new HomeKit feature

Earlier this week, Aaron Perris discovered code references to a new feature where “nearby smart home accessories could show controls in the Dynamic Island.” Now, @itspdfu has found even more details about how this feature will work.

In a new social media post today, pdfu says Apple’s “second-party” home accessories co-developed with LG will support this new “Proximity Control” feature.

When you tap or bring your iPhone near one of LG’s accessories, a notification will pop out of the Dynamic Island. The notification will show an “Open Controls” button for accessories like thermostats. For cameras and doorbells, you’ll see a “camera viewer.”

The account explains:

You’ll also see feedback in the Dynamic Island as iPhone launches setup when you first tap the accessory to pair it.

Behind the scenes, the accessory writes an “apple-deviceid” in the Matter payload stored on its NFC tag that helps iOS identify it when tapped. It also broadcasts a Bluetooth Low Energy advert for Apple Proximity Control.

You’ll seemingly have the option to turn this feature off in the Home app. As always, features referenced in Apple’s code might not ship, or they could work materially differently when they do launch.

Apple’s “second-party” LG accessories will debut another Home feature: Proximity Control.

— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 9, 2026

Still, this is a clear example of a feature that will be unique to these so-called “second-party” accessories. Bloomberg first reported on Apple’s collaboration with LG earlier this week, detailing that the two companies worked together to develop smart home products including a thermostat, deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera, and flood light camera.

by  Jess Weatherbed

Oct 12, 2026, 4:52 PM UTC

Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Elon Musk has handed out at least $276 million to Republican groups since July, The New York Times reports, making him both the party’s top known donor and the biggest established midterm donor. $158 million of that money — one of the largest political donations in American history — has been funneled into the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC that aims to secure and maintain a Republican Senate majority. Among others, it’s fighting to retain the party’s Senate seat in Texas, which serves as a major hub for Musk’s business empire.

He’s also donated over $76 million to America PAC, a super PAC Musk founded in 2024 that canvasses for hard-to-reach Republican voters. Smaller amounts have also been given to other conservative groups, including:

$20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund super PAC for House Republicans

$10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, supporting Ken Paxton’s Senate Seat bid in Texas

$10 million to the Republican Governors Association

$2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association

The roughly $366 million that Musk has donated to federal committees over the entire 2025-26 election cycle is significantly higher than the $290 million he gave out in 2024 to help President Trump return to office, when he pledged to spend “around $45 million a month.” That’s despite Musk announcing in May last year that “In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future.” He’s consistently failed to stick to that promise so far.

Fitbit Edge Specs

Display: 1.34-inch AMOLED

Charging: 24 hours of battery in 5 minutes

Water Resistance: IP68/5ATM

Phone Compatibility: Android 11+, iOS 16.4+

Bluetooth 5.4

Fitness tracking: SpO2, steps, heart rate, blood pressure/insulin trends, ECG, VO2 Max, more

Weight: 17.7g

	

The report also mentions support for Gemini, some form of Google Play integration, and that the battery is user-replaceable. 

Also notable here is that Fitbit Edge is apparently compatible with iPhone, something that it shares in common with Fitbit Air, but that the Pixel Watch series lacks. 

A release date for the Fitbit Edge remains unknown at this point, but it’s clear that the tracker is making its debut in the very near future.

title: Someone ported Pixel 11’s Rambler voice-to-text to other Android phones
snippet: One of the best new features of Google’s Pixel 11 (and Googlebook) is support for Rambler voice-to-text, and it’s now been ported to other devices – if you’re willing to take the risk, that is. more…
fullText:
One of the best new features of Google’s Pixel 11 (and Googlebook) is support for Rambler voice-to-text, and it’s now been ported to other devices – if you’re willing to take the risk, that is.

Rambler on the Pixel 11 series is essentially AI-enhanced voice-to-text. The feature takes what you say and runs it through AI, spitting out a result that includes grammar and formatting while taking out filler words and times you may have tripped over your words. It’s not perfect, as not being able to see a live preview or get word-for-word output can be a little unsettling, but it’s still a huge upgrade to traditional voice-to-text.

That’s why it can be a little annoying that it’s Pixel 11-only.

A developer, though, has managed to port the feature to any other Android phone. “PixelBoard” is a split off of the Gboard app that brings support for Rambler to essentially any other Android phone. 

	
	

In a post on Reddit (h/t Artem Russakovskii), the developer explains that the project is based on the official Gboard app, just modified to unlock Rambler and other new writing tools.

The app is available for sideloading via the project’s GitHub page, but as always that’s done at your own risk. That said, we installed the app on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 to a complete success. It runs just like Rambler on a Pixel 11. Your results may vary and, again, install at your own risk! The project has other install methods available, including patching the existing Gboard installation on your phone.

It’s still unclear if Google ever plans to bring Rambler to other devices, but third-party mods like this will be the only way to do so for the time being. For those wanting to stick with a Play Store install, Microsoft’s SwiftKey acts as a fine alternative.

title: The iPhone Duo’s Unfolding Animation Is Giving Z Fold 8 Owners FOMO, but Not Me
snippet: Commentary: While there are ways to re-create some of the iPhone Duo’s style on an Android device, it feels a little desperate to me.
fullText:
When I first got my hands on the iPhone Duo, I admittedly dismissed the unfolding animation that would soon become a highlight of online discourse. I was less interested in the smooth transition as content shifted from one screen to another and more focused on details such as the matte inner display and seemingly invisible crease.

But in the weeks since Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, which drops Oct. 23, I’ve seen countless examples on social media of people trying to recreate that buzzed-about animation on their Android foldables. While the Play Store offers plenty of launchers for customizing Android phones — including ones that mimic the iPhone’s home screen — this appears to be one iOS design element that users are particularly eager to bring to their devices.

Sometimes, you really can’t predict what people will care about most — or the lengths they’ll go to imitate a feature.

		

			

The primary phone people have used to recreate the iPhone Duo’s cascading transition effect is Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which debuted in July with a passport-size foldable design ahead of Apple’s release. Unlike iOS, Samsung’s One UI interface, which runs on top of Android on Galaxy devices, doesn’t include a folding animation. Instead, content simply transitions from the Z Fold 8’s cover screen to its inner display once the phone is opened about halfway. I never considered this a deficiency until I saw the flood of positive reactions to the iPhone Duo’s fluid transition effect. 

To bridge that gap, several creators have posted videos explaining how to use third-party apps and developer tools on GitHub to get a similar effect on the Z Fold 8, with caveats like “the smoothness and quality won’t be the same‘” and “install it [at] your own risk.” (That’s encouraging!) The steps don’t seem particularly complicated, and some options appear to have cropped up in the Play Store as well.

I’ve chosen to forgo installing these Duo-copycat apps on my precious Galaxy Z Fold 8 for two reasons. First, I’m not much of a risk-taker. Second, I’m not interested in imitating an aesthetic element of Apple’s software with a derivative version, especially when the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a standout foldable device in its own right. While the value of the Duo’s sleek animation has since grown on me, I’m not quite desperate enough to retrofit it onto a foldable phone that’s just as functional without that flourish.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 might not have a nifty opening animation by default, but I don’t see that as a deficiency.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Don’t get me wrong: I think Apple’s combination of hardware and software expertise will elevate the iPhone Duo in a way that merits the attention the phone has received, despite being relatively “late” to the foldables game. But I also think it’s more tasteful for consumers to embrace what each phone-maker does best, rather than shoehorning in a competitor’s feature for something as superficial as an animation effect. 

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is one of my favorite phones I’ve tested this year, earning it a CNET Editors’ Choice Award. Its versatile design is optimized for both vertical and horizontal content: I can stream YouTube videos and movies on the 7.6-inch inner display, then rotate it to seamlessly scroll through social posts. The crease is barely noticeable, and the battery easily lasts all day. The 5.5-inch cover screen never feels cramped, while its sharp corners give the phone a highly polished look. And despite lacking a telephoto lens, the Z Fold 8’s dual rear cameras pull their weight, capturing crisp, vibrant photos.

The iPhone Duo shares many attributes with the Z Fold 8, including a palm-size design, 7.6-inch inner display and dual rear cameras. Those similarities prompted Samsung to post a series of salty tweets after Apple debuted its foldable last month, including one that reads, “Let us know when you’re done reheating our leftovers.”

That said, I am curious how app developers might optimize their platforms for the iPhone Duo in ways we haven’t seen with other foldable phones. While the Android operating system spans a wide range of devices and configurations, iOS developers only have to cater to a single foldable, potentially leading to a more tailored and streamlined experience. We got a glimpse of how Netflix is building its app for the Duo, and it’ll be interesting to see how both Apple and other third-party developers take full advantage of the phone’s 1.4:1 aspect ratio in ways that could make its predecessors seem behind the curve in that regard.

“Borrowing” features from each other is what phone-makers do best. Down the road, it’s possible companies such as Samsung will implement foldable capabilities that Apple rolled out first, and vice versa. Heck, Apple’s delayed entry into this space means it had time to analyze what worked well for its competitors before jumping in with its own rendition. It’s just how the industry works. 

So maybe the Galaxy Z Fold 9 — or whatever Samsung decides to call the follow-up to the Z Fold 8 — will have its own nifty opening animation. But until Samsung itself embraces the idea, I’ll stick with using the standout foldable as-is.

title: Google Wallet for Android getting vertically stacked card list [U]
snippet: Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list. more…
fullText:
Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list.

Update 10/6: This revamp is not yet widely rolled out, but we’re slowly seeing it on more devices.

With this stacked redesign, you’ll see one full card preview and the sliver of a second at the top. To expand, you can tap or swipe down to enter the fullscreen view (as seen below). After selecting a card, you can tap-to-pay.

To see card details and transaction history, select the new settings gear icon in the top-right corner. This is more cumbersome than the current design. 

	

	

Original 9/14: The current design shows your saved credit and debit cards as a carousel at the top of the screen. You swipe horizontally to browse, with this approach showing just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google lets you reorder the payment methods and set a default card. This interface allows passes to share the homepage.

The new design uses a vertical list, like the Wallet app on iPhone, that really benefits those with multiple saved cards. Google is showing much more of the card design than Apple, which is a nice aspect of the current look.

This approach is definitely friendlier for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom.

There are a handful of reports about this rollout over the weekend, with most coming from international users.

title: Apple partners with The King’s Trust on new Creative Labs initiative in the UK
snippet: Apple and The King’s Trust announced today an expansion of their partnership with a new education program that offers workshops to help young people build creative and digital skills. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple and The King’s Trust announced today an expansion of their partnership with a new education program that offers workshops to help young people build creative and digital skills. Here are the details.

Apple’s partnership with The King’s Trust dates back to 2019

In a Newsroom post published today, Apple and The King’s Trust announced the “Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs” initiative, which will “offer young people meaningful engagement with Apple experts across industries as they explore a variety of career pathways, equipping them with the technology, resources, skills, confidence, and expertise needed to realize their potential.”

According to Apple, the program’s immersive educational experience began earlier this week with “music industry and creative workshops, aligned to the recent opening of Apple Music Hall.”

Apple says the first cohort will include up to 20 participants aged 18 to 30, with additional sessions and cohorts planned over the next year.

Here’s Alisha Johnson Wilder, Apple’s senior director of Global Community Impact, on what the initiative means for Apple and its partnership with The King’s Trust:

“At Apple, we believe education is a powerful force for equity and opportunity. […] For years, we’ve been proud to work alongside The King’s Trust to spark creativity and open doors for young people across the UK. With the launch of the Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs, we’re taking that commitment further, connecting the next generation of creators and innovators directly with our experts, technology, and mentorship to help them build vital skills, discover their passions, and thrive in the workforce.”

Jonathan Townsend, The King’s Trust’s UK chief executive, also commented on the initiative, calling it “an exciting new chapter in our partnership that will help even more young people develop the confidence and creative digital skills they need to take their next steps toward employment.”

In the announcement, Apple said it is also working with The King’s Trust on resources to improve AI literacy and help educators incorporate new technologies into their teaching.

title: Silent Hill Townfall Is Real for Me: I’ve Been to the Actual St. Amelia
snippet: In this spoiler-free review, I explain why this is the most personal horror game I’ve ever played
fullText:
I’ve just finished playing Silent Hill: Townfall, and it’s a masterclass on what a modern horror game can be. At least, it is for me. From its perfectly observed setting in Scotland to an all-too-real sense of a community that’s collapsed in the face of a disaster, this game grabbed me on a deeply personal level and pulled me in as no other Silent Hill game has done before. 

Set in the fictional Scottish harbor town of St Amelia in 1996, Silent Hill: Townfall follows the journey of Simon Ordell, who, after pulling himself out of the sea at the start of the game, proceeds to unravel the mystery of what’s happened in the town, what role he played and crucially how he can put things right. 

Simon washes up in St Amelia with no idea what’s going on.Konami

From the shambling monsters with planks morphing out of their heads to the impenetrable fog obscuring most of your way forward, Townfall is in many ways classic Silent Hill despite being something of a smaller-scoped spinoff, much like last year’s Silent Hill f. Like its predecessors, gameplay relies on puzzle-solving, exploration and using a mixture of stealth and combat (using limited resources) to either avoid or take down enemies. 

			

More from CNET

So, par for the course for Silent Hill then? In many ways, yes; there’s certainly enough hallmarks of the franchise to keep regulars happy and, much like I found in 2017’s Resident Evil 7, a shift from an over-the-shoulder to a first-person perspective only helps to immerse you more in the game. 

Simon’s journey is largely one of discovery. With no memories of what’s going on or why he’s in this deserted village, the game instead drip-feeds you nuggets of information — often simply through emails on computers, newspaper clippings or other pieces of environmental storytelling, many of which are easy to miss. But by slowing down and taking the time to explore the game world and pick up clues, you start to feel connected with Simon as he constructs his story. 

Simon has no idea what’s going on and, for most of the game, nor will you.Konami

It’s not a unique take on Silent Hill by any means, and I don’t expect Townfall to necessarily pull in a fresh audience that’s never played a title before. But it’s got more than enough meat on its bones to keep existing fans happy and to tempt back those of you who’ve written the series off in recent years. 

But there’s much more than a fresh perspective that pulled me into Townfall.

The setting of St Amelia is based on a real seaside town, called St Monan’s — a town that’s only about an hour’s drive from my home in Edinburgh and somewhere I have visited many times. While the layout isn’t a direct replication, there are numerous elements I immediately recognized from the real-life town. Considering the game was developed by the Glasgow-based developer Screen Burn Games, this fidelity to a Scottish setting is unsurprising but welcome.

Not a screenshot from the game, but from a video I shot when I visited the real St Amelia at night.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The architecture, the scattered fishing nets and lobster pots along the harbor front, the bunting strewn around the streets — all present and accurate to real-life seaside Scotland. I recognize elements of nearby North Berwick too, and there’s even a reference to the “award-winning Amelia Fish Bar” which I can only assume is a direct nod to the actually award-winning Anstruther Fish Bar, which you’ll find about a 10-minute drive from St Monans. 

Even the more modern details reminiscent of towns redeveloped in the 1960s are perfectly observed, down to the phones, the office equipment and the Microsoft Word Art used on community noticeboard posters — and will be immediately recognizable to anyone, like me, who grew up in Britain in the 90s. When I visited St Monans earlier in the year to photograph the town, I focused my attention on a 1980s phone box, which struck me at the time as being “very Silent Hill”. Unsurprisingly, I found that identical boxes featured heavily in the game world.

This 1980s phonebox, seen here in real-life St Monans, features heavily in the game.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The result of all this is that St. Amelia feels like a place I’ve already been to, wandered around and actively enjoyed as I ate fish and chips on the harbor wall with family and friends. I felt a deep sense of familiarity walking around in the game, which made it all the more jarring to see the beautiful, tranquil place I knew transformed into a landscape of horror and terror. 

It was an amazing — albeit disturbing — sensation to feel so personally connected with an in-game setting, but it’s not one that everyone will have. I played through most of last year’s Silent Hill f and while I broadly enjoyed the game, its admittedly interesting 1960s rural Japan setting didn’t immerse me in the same way because I’ve never been, so I lack any frame of reference. Ditto for the Silent Hill 2 remake set in the US state of Maine. It’s not that I can’t enjoy any media that I don’t have a personal connection with (I’ve never been to Connecticut but it doesn’t stop me enjoying Gilmore Girls), but having a game based essentially in your own backyard is a great way to feel a much deeper sense of immersion in what’s going on. 

But there’s another connection that many more of us can appreciate. 

You’ll be using a portable TV —  a classic bit of 90s tech — to keep out of the way of enemies.Konami

The COVID factor

The game is set in the 1990s, so COVID-19 isn’t something it references in any way. But something’s happened here. Something that has brought a town to its knees and I’m damn sure that the game’s developer,  Screen Burn, kept its memories of the pandemic firmly in mind when it was building its game world. 

Shops and pharmacies lay empty, shelves are stripped of all essentials. Emergency aid stations have been set up, while flyers and posters around the village describe overstretched medical staff and a lack of supplies, advising to the population to stay at home. Sound familiar? 

Walking around the empty, silent town, I was struck by how similar the game world felt to my own experiences of the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in the early days. I didn’t know how widespread things were, or if we were safe at all. Silent Hill: Townfall perfectly captures that sense of foreboding and taps into our lingering memories of those difficult days. 

Messages like this are common in the game and are very reminiscent of similar signs from the Covid days.Konami

I vividly remember walking down Edinburgh’s famous Royal Mile on a Saturday in March 2020. There happened to be an extremely Silent Hill-like fog draped over the city and the usually bustling street was almost empty, apart from me. It was deeply unsettling to see, and I can still remember that real sense of unease as I walked down the cobblestones, each step echoing out far louder than usual. 

At the time, I even texted my brother saying that it feels like “something from Silent Hill” — and having played Townfall, I think I was spot on. Walking around Townfall’s mist-shrouded St Amelia, seeing the empty streets, the closed businesses and the solitary figures in the distance felt like reliving my own memories. 

In the daytime, St Monans is an idyllic place to visitAndrew Lanxon/CNET

Sure, most people playing the game probably haven’t been to St Monans in real life, so you may not have that same sense of familiarity. Maybe you’ve not even been to Scotland, or the UK, or even left your hometown. So much of the game’s effect on me may well be lost on you. But for me, that’s always the joy of playing some games or watching certain movies — settings, storylines or characters will resonate with us differently depending on our own backgrounds and experiences.

For me, Silent Hill: Townfall hit hard, not just because of its Scottish setting but because of its ability to conjure up real memories from a dark time that we all lived through. That one-two punch meant I connected with this game on a much deeper level than I anticipated and resulted in my enjoying Townfall more than any other Silent Hill game I’ve played. It’s rare to have horror set in your own backyard — especially when it directly evokes memories of your own home being warped by haunting calamity.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Andrew Lanxon
						

						

							Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe						
					

											

								

											When he's not testing the latest phones or phone cameras, Andrew can normally be found with his own camera in hand or behind his drums or eating his stash of home-cooked food -- sometimes all at once.

title: Why did it take so long for someone to make a magnetic USB-C port? [Video]
snippet: In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything. more…
fullText:
In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is a full-on powerhouse with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chipset, up to 128GB of RAM, and plenty of ports. But it’s one of those ports that is the most unique new features.

“Magnetic Connect” is Microsoft’s name for “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C” charging port. The USB-C port itself functions as normal with any standard cable, but the included charger is specially designed to magnetically attach akin to Apple’s MagSafe or any other number of magnetic charging connectors.

I want it.

	

The “how” here is that the charging portion of the cable uses super-strong magnets to align and latch on the charger so the port connects properly, but the charger itself also tapers the edges of the USB-C port so it can more easily slide into place. As such, that end won’t securely connect to your phone or other devices, as it needs that magnet to hold itself in place. 

	

The Verge shows it in action in a video on YouTube:

Microsoft is apparently hoping this idea will catch on and show up on other laptops, and I sure hope that’s the case! As for phones, the size of the magnets implies it probably won’t be feasible in a standard smartphone, but I really hope this idea starts showing up everywhere! Certainly I hope it at least shows up on a laptop that doesn’t cost $2,600 — Surface Laptop Ultra pre-orders are open now.

What do you think?

title: Sketchy rumor again says OLED iPad mini will lack one key feature
snippet: Apple is widely expected to introduce a new OLED iPad mini as soon as later this month. A sketchy new rumor today once again claims the new iPad mini will switch to OLED but still have a 60Hz refresh rate and lack ProMotion support. more…
fullText:
Apple is widely expected to introduce a new OLED iPad mini as soon as later this month. A sketchy new rumor today once again claims the new iPad mini will switch to OLED but still have a 60Hz refresh rate and lack ProMotion support.

This is the second time we’ve heard this rumor, but both times it has come from the same source: the yeux1122 account on Naver. This account has a very mixed track record with Apple rumors. It often seems to regurgitate information from unnamed sources rather than provide its own.

Nonetheless, the latest post from yeux1122 claims “there is mention of 120Hz in some overseas sources” for the new OLED iPad mini, but “domestic production volume has already confirmed” it will use a 60Hz display.

Again, I’m treating this rumor with more than a healthy dose of skepticism, since no other reliable sources have corroborated it.

However, if it does come to fruition, this will be a disappointing limitation for iPad mini buyers. This iPad mini upgrade is expected to bring a number of other notable improvements, including:

An OLED display.

Apple’s A20 Pro chip, up from the current iPad mini’s A17 Pro chip.

A refreshed design with smaller bezels that could be more water-resistant.

The FaceTime camera will be relocated to the horizontal bezel, similar to Apple’s other iPad models.

	

If Apple made all those changes but stopped short of upgrading the display to ProMotion with a 120Hz refresh rate, it’d really sour the launch of the new iPad mini.

The new iPad mini is expected to launch later this month, so we don’t have much longer to wait to know for sure.

What do you think? Will the new iPad mini have ProMotion and 120Hz refresh rates? Let us know down in the comments.
